java-spring-q1.testing: whether you can go past "hash table with linked lists" to the hash spread, the tree bins and the resize, with the constants.
java-spring-q1.trap: stopping at "collisions go into a linked list". The treeify threshold is the follow-up.
java-spring-q1.spoken:
Beat Say
1 · The one-line claim "A HashMap is an array of buckets. The key's hash picks the bucket, and keys that land in the same bucket are chained inside it."
2 · How it works "On put, it takes hashCode, mixes the high bits into the low bits, and masks with capacity minus one to get an index. If the bucket is empty the node goes in. If not, it walks the chain comparing hash, then equals: a match replaces the value, otherwise the node is appended. When a chain reaches eight nodes and the table has at least sixty-four buckets, that bucket becomes a red-black tree."
3 · Prove it "The strings 'Aa' and 'BB' have the same hashCode, two thousand one hundred and twelve. Both go to bucket zero, and both are still found, because equals tells them apart."
4 · What it costs or breaks "When the size passes capacity times the load factor of zero point seven five, the table doubles and entries are redistributed. And it isn't thread-safe: concurrent writes can lose entries or corrupt the structure."
5 · So what for the system "So lookups are constant time on average, logarithmic in the worst bucket. I give keys a good, stable hashCode, presize maps that I know will be large, and use ConcurrentHashMap when threads share it."
Close "Hash, spread, bucket, chain, tree at eight, resize at three-quarters full."

stages.name: The one-line claim
How it works
stages.html:
put(k, v):hashCodespreadindexempty? insertelse walk: same hash and equals? replaceelse appendtreeify or resize if needed
Constant Value Meaning
default capacity 16 always a power of two, so hash & (n − 1) works as modulo
load factor 0.75 resize when size exceeds capacity × 0.75
treeify threshold 8 a chain this long becomes a red-black tree
minimum treeify capacity 64 below this the table resizes instead of treeifying
untreeify threshold 6 a shrinking tree bin turns back into a chain

Why spread the hash: with a small table only the low bits choose the bucket. XOR-ing in the high 16 bits lets them take part, which reduces clustering from poor hash functions.

stages.name: Prove it
stages.html:
Prove it — JDK 25:

import java.util.*;
class Demo {
    static int spread(Object k) { int h = k.hashCode(); return h ^ (h >>> 16); }   // HashMap.hash()
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        System.out.println("Aa".hashCode() + " " + "BB".hashCode());              // equal hash codes
        int n = 16;                                                             // default capacity
        System.out.println("bucket of Aa: " + ((n - 1) & spread("Aa")) + ", of BB: " + ((n - 1) & spread("BB")));
        Map<String, Integer> m = new HashMap<>();
        m.put("Aa", 1); m.put("BB", 2);                                          // same bucket, equals() differs
        System.out.println(m.get("Aa") + " " + m.get("BB") + " size=" + m.size());
        System.out.println("resize threshold: " + (int) (16 * 0.75f));
    }
}
// → 2112 2112
// → bucket of Aa: 0, of BB: 0
// → 1 2 size=2
// → resize threshold: 12
Line Shows
1 different strings, equal hash codes
2 so both map to the same bucket
3 both values are still retrieved: equals separates keys inside a bucket
4 a default map resizes on the 13th entry

stages.name: What it costs or breaks
stages.html:
Event Cost Note
lookup, average O(1) one bucket, short chain
lookup, worst bucket O(log n) with tree bins, O(n) before Java 8 tree bins defend against hash-collision attacks
resize O(n), every entry visited doubling means each entry stays or moves by exactly the old capacity
concurrent writes undefined: lost updates, corrupted bins before Java 8, concurrent resize could loop for ever

Treeification is a defence, not the normal path: with a decent hash function chains of eight are extremely rare.

stages.name: So what for the system
stages.html:
Practice Why
immutable keys with consistent equals and hashCode the hash is used at insert and at every lookup
presize: new HashMap<>(expected / 0.75 + 1) avoids repeated resizes while loading
ConcurrentHashMap for shared maps HashMap gives no guarantees under concurrent writes
LinkedHashMap or TreeMap when order matters HashMap iteration order is unspecified and changes on resize

Thread-safety: HashMap is not thread-safe. Read-only sharing after safe publication is fine.

followUps.question: Why is the capacity always a power of two?
followUps.html:
So the index is a bit mask instead of a division, and resize splits buckets cleanly.

index = hash & (n − 1)            ← valid only when n is a power of two
on doubling: a node stays at i, or moves to i + old capacity, decided by one bit

followUps.question: "Collisions go in a linked list, so worst case is O(n)."
followUps.html:
Not since Java 8.

Version Long bucket Worst lookup
Java 7 linked list O(n)
Java 8+ red-black tree at 8 nodes (table ≥ 64) O(log n)

followUps.question: A default HashMap holds 12 entries. What happens on the 13th put?
followUps.html:
The table doubles to 32 buckets.

threshold = 16 × 0.75 = 12      size becomes 13 > 12  →  resize to 32, new threshold 24

followUps.question: What if hashCode returns a constant?
followUps.html:
Everything lands in one bucket; the map still works, slowly.

  • Correctness holds, because equals still distinguishes keys.
  • Performance degrades to a tree lookup, and only if keys are Comparable does the tree order them usefully.

followUps.question: Where has this caused a production problem?
followUps.html:
Three recurring shapes.

Incident Cause
CPU pinned at 100% a HashMap shared and written by several threads
entries that can't be found a key mutated after insertion
latency spikes during load a huge map growing by repeated resize

dontSay: "It's a hash table with linked lists" — and nothing about tree bins or resize.
"HashMap is O(1)" without "on average".
"It's fine across threads if you only put."

java-spring-q2.testing: whether you can trace the lookup to the wrong bucket and name the consequence: an entry that is stranded, which is a memory leak.
java-spring-q2.trap: "it just won't be found", without saying the entry is still there and can never be removed.
java-spring-q2.spoken:
Beat Say
1 · Predict it out loud "Putting it in works. If I then change a field that hashCode uses, get returns null, containsKey returns false, and the map's size is still one."
2 · Trace the mechanism "The bucket was chosen from the hash at insertion. After the mutation the key hashes to a different bucket, so the lookup probes the wrong place. Even a fresh key with the old value fails: it reaches the right bucket, but equals against the mutated key is now false."
3 · The rule that decides it "The rule is that a key's hashCode and equals must not change while it is in the map."
4 · Variants that flip it "Mutating a field that isn't part of equals or hashCode is harmless. Removing the key, changing it, and putting it back is the correct way to change it."
5 · The production version "In production this is a leak: the entry is unreachable by lookup and by remove, and only iteration can see it. So I use immutable keys: strings, records, enums, or value objects with final fields."
Close "Hash at insert, mutation moves the true hash, the entry is stranded. Keys should be immutable."

stages.name: Predict it out loud
stages.html:
Prove it — JDK 25:

import java.util.*;
class Demo {
    static class Key {
        String id; Key(String id) { this.id = id; }
        @Override public boolean equals(Object o) { return o instanceof Key k && k.id.equals(id); }
        @Override public int hashCode() { return id.hashCode(); }
    }
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        Map<Key, String> m = new HashMap<>();
        Key k = new Key("order-1");
        m.put(k, "paid");
        k.id = "order-2";                                   // mutate the key while it is in the map
        System.out.println(m.get(k));                       // probes the bucket of the new hash
        System.out.println(m.get(new Key("order-1")));      // right bucket, but equals() now fails
        System.out.println(m.containsKey(k) + " size=" + m.size());
    }
}
// → null
// → null
// → false size=1
Call Result Why
get(k) with the mutated key null it hashes to a different bucket
get(new Key("order-1")) null right bucket, but equals with the stored (mutated) key fails
containsKey(k), size() false, 1 the entry exists and can't be reached

stages.name: Trace the mechanism
stages.claim: the lookup probes the wrong bucket
stages.html:
At insert:hash("order-1")bucket Anode stored in A, with that hash cached in the node
After mutation:hash("order-2")bucket Bemptynull
With a fresh "order-1" key:bucket Anode foundequals? stored key is now "order-2"falsenull

The node also caches the old hash, so even landing in the same bucket by chance would fail the hash comparison first.

stages.name: The rule that decides it
stages.claim: stable hash and equality while stored
stages.html:
Contract Requirement
hashCode the same value for as long as the object is used as a key
equals consistent with hashCode: equal objects have equal hash codes
both built from the same fields

The same rule applies to elements of a HashSet, which is a HashMap underneath.

stages.name: Variants that flip it
stages.html:
Variant Result
mutate a field not used by equals or hashCode safe
remove(k), mutate, put(k, v) safe: the entry is re-bucketed
key in a TreeMap, mutate the compared field broken in the same way: the tree's ordering is now wrong
key in an IdentityHashMap safe: it uses reference identity and System.identityHashCode
mutate the value always safe

stages.name: The production version
stages.html:
Symptom Cause
a cache that grows though "entries are removed" remove can't find the mutated keys
a session or deduplication set that lets duplicates through the mutated element is no longer found
heap dump shows a large HashMap with entries nobody can look up stranded nodes
Guards:records or final fields for key typesno setters on anything used in hashCodea code-review rule for collections keyed by entities

JPA note: an entity whose hashCode uses a generated ID changes hash when it is persisted. Use a stable business key, or a constant-per-class hash with ID-based equals.

followUps.question: Why is String such a good key?
followUps.html:
It is immutable, and it caches its hash.

  • Immutable: the hash can never change after insertion.
  • Cached hash: computed once per instance.
  • Well-distributed hashCode and a fast equals.

followUps.question: "The entry is gone after the mutation."
followUps.html:
It is still there, holding memory.

Operation Sees the entry?
get, containsKey, remove no
size, iteration over entrySet yes

That gap is why it is a leak and not a deletion.

followUps.question: Can I recover the stranded entry?
followUps.html:
Only by iterating, or by rebuilding the map.

iterate entrySet ─▶ iterator.remove() on the bad entry, or copy everything into a new HashMap so keys are re-hashed

followUps.question: How would you write the key class?
followUps.html:
As a record, or a final class with final fields.

record OrderKey(String tenantId, long orderId) { }      // equals, hashCode, immutability generated

followUps.question: How do you find this in a running service?
followUps.html:
From a heap dump and from the key type.

  • Heap dump: a map whose size keeps growing; its key class has setters.
  • Code search: mutable classes used as map keys or set elements.
  • Prevent: a static-analysis rule flagging non-final fields in hashCode.

dontSay: "It won't be found" — and stop there.
"Just override hashCode properly" — the override is the problem if its fields change.
"Use the entity as the key" without thinking about generated IDs.

java-spring-q3.testing: whether you know the mechanism (modCount against a snapshot or weakly consistent view) and that "fail-safe" doesn't mean "consistent".
java-spring-q3.trap: calling fail-safe iteration "thread-safe with full consistency", or building logic on catching the exception.
java-spring-q3.spoken:
Beat Say
1 · Frame the axis "It is about what an iterator does when the collection changes underneath it: complain, or carry on with a view that may be stale."
2 · Where fail-fast fits "ArrayList and HashMap iterators are fail-fast. The collection keeps a modification count; the iterator remembers it and throws ConcurrentModificationException if it changed. That is best effort, a bug detector, not a guarantee."
3 · Where fail-safe fits "The concurrent collections don't throw. CopyOnWriteArrayList iterates the array as it was when the iterator was created. ConcurrentHashMap's iterator is weakly consistent: it may or may not show concurrent changes."
4 · The deciding question "So I ask: is this collection shared between threads, and what is the ratio of reads to writes?"
5 · What I'd pick here "Single-threaded code keeps the ordinary collections, and removes during iteration with removeIf or the iterator's own remove. Shared, read-mostly lists use copy-on-write. Shared maps use ConcurrentHashMap, accepting a possibly stale view."
Close "Fail-fast tells you about a bug; fail-safe tolerates concurrency at the price of freshness or of copying."

stages.name: Frame the axis
stages.claim: throw, or show a possibly stale view
stages.html:
Fail-fast Fail-safe (weakly consistent or snapshot)
Examples ArrayList, HashMap, HashSet CopyOnWriteArrayList, ConcurrentHashMap, ConcurrentLinkedQueue
On concurrent change ConcurrentModificationException no exception
Mechanism compares modCount with the value saved at creation iterates a snapshot, or tolerates changes
View current, or it throws may be stale
Cost none copying per write (COW), or weaker guarantees

stages.name: Where fail-fast fits
stages.html:
Prove it — JDK 25:

import java.util.*;
import java.util.concurrent.CopyOnWriteArrayList;
class Demo {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        List<Integer> list = new ArrayList<>(List.of(1, 2, 3, 4));
        try { for (Integer x : list) if (x == 2) list.remove(x); }
        catch (ConcurrentModificationException e) { System.out.println("fail-fast: " + e.getClass().getSimpleName()); }
        list.removeIf(x -> x == 3);                           // the supported way
        System.out.println(list);
        List<Integer> cow = new CopyOnWriteArrayList<>(List.of(1, 2, 3));
        for (Integer x : cow) if (x == 1) cow.add(99);        // iterates the snapshot taken at start
        System.out.println(cow);
    }
}
// → fail-fast: ConcurrentModificationException
// → [1, 4]
// → [1, 2, 3, 99]
The check:iterator createdsaves expectedModCounteach next() compares it with modCountdifferent? throw
Fact Consequence
it fires in single-threaded code too list.remove(x) inside a for-each is the usual cause
it is best effort under real concurrency a change can be missed; never rely on the exception
the supported ways to remove Iterator.remove(), removeIf, or collect and remove afterwards

stages.name: Where fail-safe fits
stages.html:
Collection What the iterator sees Cost
CopyOnWriteArrayList the array as it was when the iterator was created every write copies the whole array
ConcurrentHashMap elements at or after creation; concurrent updates may or may not appear none per write; no global consistency
ConcurrentLinkedQueue weakly consistent —

In the snippet, 99 was added during iteration and the loop didn't visit it: the iterator was reading the old array.

stages.name: The deciding question
stages.html:
Situation Choice
one thread plain collection; remove with removeIf
shared, many reads, rare writes (listeners, config) CopyOnWriteArrayList
shared map, frequent writes ConcurrentHashMap
need a consistent snapshot of a shared map copy it under a lock, or use an immutable copy that is swapped
shared, write-heavy list a concurrent queue or a lock: copy-on-write would be too costly

stages.name: What I'd pick here
stages.html:
Single thread: list.removeIf(predicate)

Shared listeners:CopyOnWriteArrayListiteration needs no lockwrites are rare
Shared counters or caches:ConcurrentHashMapcompound updates through compute or merge

Thread-safety: fail-safe iteration is safe to run concurrently with writers. It is not a transaction: totals computed while others write can be wrong.

followUps.question: What exactly is modCount?
followUps.html:
A counter of structural modifications.

Counts Doesn't count
add, remove, clear, resize replacing a value for an existing key; set(i, x) on a list

followUps.question: "Fail-safe iterators give a consistent, thread-safe view."
followUps.html:
Thread-safe, yes. Consistent, only for the snapshot kind, and that view is old.

Kind Consistency
snapshot (COW) consistent as of iterator creation
weakly consistent (CHM) no single point in time

followUps.question: Removing the second-to-last element in a for-each doesn't throw. Why?
followUps.html:
Because hasNext() returns false before the check in next() can run.

list [1, 2, 3], remove 2 while on it  →  size is 2, cursor is 2  →  hasNext() is false  →  loop ends, no exception

It is the proof that the exception is best effort.

followUps.question: Does Collections.synchronizedList make iteration safe?
followUps.html:
No. Each call is synchronised, but iteration is many calls.

synchronized (list) { for (var x : list) … } ─▶ the caller must hold the lock for the whole loop

followUps.question: When has copy-on-write hurt in production?
followUps.html:
When someone used it for a list that is written often.

Symptom Cause
allocation rate and GC pressure spike the whole array is copied on each add
CPU in Arrays.copyOf large list, frequent writes

It is a read-mostly structure; a profile showing array copies is the giveaway.

dontSay: "Catch ConcurrentModificationException and retry."
"Fail-safe means always up to date."
"Use a synchronized list and iterate normally."

java-spring-q4.testing: whether you can describe the container without the word "magic": a registry of definitions, a dependency graph, and often a proxy.
java-spring-q4.trap: "a bean is any Java object". The distinction is who owns the lifecycle.
java-spring-q4.spoken:
Beat Say
1 · Plain definition "A bean is an object whose lifecycle the Spring container owns: it creates it, wires its dependencies, and destroys it. An object I create with new is not a bean, even if it is the same class."
2 · What the container does "At startup the container collects bean definitions from component scanning, from at-Bean methods and from imports. It then resolves the dependency graph: for each bean it finds what the constructor needs, creates those first, injects them, runs post-processors and initialisation callbacks, and may wrap the result in a proxy."
3 · Where it breaks "It breaks in predictable ways: no bean of a required type, two candidates for one injection point, a circular dependency, or advice that doesn't apply because the call bypassed the proxy."
4 · How I use it "I use constructor injection, so dependencies are explicit and final, the object is always valid, and the class is testable with plain new. And singletons stay stateless."
5 · Adjacent concept "The next thing to know is the lifecycle, because the proxy is created near its end, and that explains most surprises with at-Transactional."
Close "A registry, a graph resolution, and often a proxy on top: inversion of control, not magic."

stages.name: Plain definition
stages.html:
Plain object Spring bean
Created by your new the container
Dependencies supplied by you the container
Lifecycle callbacks, proxies none applied by the container
Scope whatever holds the reference singleton by default

Inversion of control: the class declares what it needs; it doesn't go and find it.

stages.name: What the container does
stages.html:
Startup:read definitionsregister BeanDefinitionsresolve the graphinstantiateinjectpost-process and initialiseready
Source of definitions Example
component scanning @Component, @Service, @Repository, @Controller
Java configuration @Bean methods in a @Configuration class
imports and auto-configuration @Import, Boot's conditional configurations 
@Service
class OrderService {
    private final PaymentGateway gateway;          // resolved by type from the registry
    OrderService(PaymentGateway gateway) { this.gateway = gateway; }
}

Trace — creating OrderService:

Step Container action
1 finds the definition, sees one constructor needing PaymentGateway
2 looks up a bean of that type; creates it first if it doesn't exist yet
3 calls the constructor with it
4 runs post-processors; wraps in a proxy if any advice applies
5 stores the singleton and hands the same instance to everyone who asks

stages.name: Where it breaks
stages.html:
Failure Message to recognise Cause
no candidate NoSuchBeanDefinitionException the class isn't scanned, or a condition excluded it
two candidates NoUniqueBeanDefinitionException several beans of the type: use @Primary or @Qualifier
cycle BeanCurrentlyInCreationException A needs B needs A through constructors
silent: advice missing no error a call that bypasses the proxy

The first three fail at startup, which is the desirable kind of failure.

stages.name: How I use it
stages.html:
Practice Why
constructor injection fields final; no half-built object; a unit test is new Service(fake)
stateless singleton beans one instance serves every thread
configuration in @ConfigurationProperties typed and validated at startup
beans at the boundaries, plain objects inside not every class needs to be a bean

Thread-safety: a singleton bean is shared by all request threads. Mutable fields in it are shared mutable state.

stages.name: Adjacent concept
stages.html:
Lifecycle:instantiateinjectaware callbackspost-process beforeinitpost-process after: proxy createdreadydestroy

What other beans receive is often the proxy, not your instance. That one fact explains why @Transactional, @Async and @Cacheable do nothing on a call made through this.

followUps.question: BeanFactory or ApplicationContext?
followUps.html:
ApplicationContext is a BeanFactory plus the features applications need.

BeanFactory ApplicationContext
Core DI yes yes
Events, resources, environment, eager singletons, post-processor auto-registration no yes

followUps.question: "Any object in a Spring application is a bean."
followUps.html:
Only objects the container created and manages.

new OrderService(…) inside a methodnot a beanno injection, no proxy, no @Transactional

followUps.question: Two implementations of one interface are on the classpath.
followUps.html:
Injection by type is ambiguous, so you choose.

Tool Use
@Primary one default
@Qualifier("name") pick at the injection point
inject List<T> or Map<String, T> get all of them

followUps.question: @Component or @Bean?
followUps.html:
@Component for your own classes, @Bean for objects you construct yourself.

  • @Component: the class is discovered by scanning.
  • @Bean: a method builds the object: third-party classes, conditional or parameterised construction.

followUps.question: What does the container cost?
followUps.html:
Startup time and memory, in exchange for wiring and cross-cutting behaviour.

Cost Mitigation
reflection and scanning at startup narrow scan packages; AOT processing; lazy initialisation where safe
indirection when debugging know the lifecycle; use the conditions report

dontSay: "Spring magically injects things."
"A bean is just an object."
"I use field injection because it's shorter."

java-spring-q5.testing: whether you know that injection happens once, so a shorter-lived bean inside a singleton doesn't refresh.
java-spring-q5.trap: expecting a prototype bean injected into a singleton to be new on every call.
java-spring-q5.spoken:
Beat Say
1 · Plain definition "A scope says how many instances of a bean exist and how long each lives."
2 · The scopes "Singleton is the default: one instance per container. Prototype gives a new instance every time the container is asked. In web applications there are also request, session and application scopes."
3 · Where it breaks "The trap is in the default. A singleton is created once and its dependencies are injected once. So if I inject a prototype into a singleton, the singleton gets one instance and keeps it for ever. The prototype never refreshes."
4 · How I fix it "The fix is to ask the container each time: inject an ObjectProvider and call getObject, use at-Lookup, or declare the shorter-lived bean with a scoped proxy, which looks up the right instance on each call. That proxy is how a request-scoped bean can be injected into a singleton at all."
5 · Adjacent concept "The related rule: singletons are shared by every thread, so they must be stateless."
Close "Scope is lifetime; injection is once; a shorter-lived dependency needs a provider or a proxy."

stages.name: Plain definition
stages.html:
"How many, and for how long."

Question Answered by scope
how many instances exist? one, one per request, one per ask
who destroys it? the container, or nobody
is it shared between threads? singleton and application: yes

stages.name: The scopes
stages.html:
Scope Instances Destroy callbacks run? Typical use
singleton (default) one per container yes stateless services, repositories
prototype a new one per lookup no: the container doesn't track them stateful helpers, builders
request one per HTTP request yes per-request context
session one per HTTP session yes user session state
application one per ServletContext yes shared web-app state

stages.name: Where it breaks
stages.html:
Prove it — a plain-Java analogue of what the container does (JDK 25):

import java.util.function.Supplier;
class Demo {
    static int created = 0;
    static class Cart { final int id = ++created; }                     // stands in for a prototype bean
    static class WrongService { final Cart cart; WrongService(Cart c) { cart = c; } }               // injected once
    static class RightService { final Supplier<Cart> carts; RightService(Supplier<Cart> s) { carts = s; } }
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        WrongService wrong = new WrongService(new Cart());
        System.out.println("injected once: " + wrong.cart.id + ", " + wrong.cart.id);
        RightService right = new RightService(Cart::new);                // ObjectProvider plays this role
        System.out.println("provider:      " + right.carts.get().id + ", " + right.carts.get().id);
    }
}
// → injected once: 1, 1
// → provider:      2, 3
Wiring Calls see
prototype injected directly into a singleton the same instance every time (1, 1)
a provider injected, asked on each call a new instance each time (2, 3)
Why:singleton created at startupconstructor called onceone prototype instance capturedreused for the life of the application

stages.name: How I fix it
stages.html:
@Service
class CheckoutService {
    private final ObjectProvider<Cart> carts;                 // a handle, not an instance
    CheckoutService(ObjectProvider<Cart> carts) { this.carts = carts; }
    void checkout() { Cart cart = carts.getObject(); /* a fresh prototype */ }
}

@Component @RequestScope                                       // scoped proxy: resolved per request
class RequestContext { /* user, tenant, trace id */ }
Fix How it works Pick when
ObjectProvider<T> explicit lookup on each call you want it visible in the code
@Lookup method the container overrides the method to do the lookup legacy code, abstract methods
scoped proxy (@RequestScope, proxyMode) the injected object is a proxy that delegates to the current instance request or session beans inside singletons

stages.name: Adjacent concept
stages.html:
Field in a singleton Verdict
final reference to another bean fine
immutable configuration fine
a mutable counter, list or "current user" a race: every request thread shares it

Thread-safety: per-request data belongs in method parameters, a request-scoped bean, or a properly propagated context. Never in a singleton field.

followUps.question: How does a scoped proxy find the right instance?
followUps.html:
Each call on the proxy looks up the bean in the current scope's store.

call on proxycurrent request attributes (thread-bound)the instance for this requestdelegate

followUps.question: "Prototype means a new object every time I use it."
followUps.html:
Every time the container is asked, not every time a field is used.

Access New instance?
context.getBean(Cart.class), provider.getObject() yes
using a field that was injected once no

followUps.question: A request-scoped bean is used from an @Async method.
followUps.html:
It fails or sees nothing: the request scope is bound to the request thread.

  • The async thread has no request attributes.
  • Pass the values as method arguments, or propagate the context deliberately.

followUps.question: Who cleans up a prototype bean?
followUps.html:
You do. The container hands it over and forgets it.

Scope @PreDestroy called by the container
singleton, request, session yes
prototype no

followUps.question: When is a non-singleton scope a design smell?
followUps.html:
When it is used to carry state that should be a parameter.

Smell Better
prototype beans holding per-call data a plain object created with new
session-scoped beans in a stateless, horizontally scaled API a token or an external store

dontSay: "Prototype gives me a fresh one each call" — not through an injected field.
"Singletons are thread-safe" — only if they are stateless.
"Request scope works anywhere" — only on a thread bound to a request.

java-spring-q6.testing: whether you name the compile error and the three resolution rules instead of guessing an order.
java-spring-q6.spoken:
Beat Say
1 · Predict it out loud "It doesn't compile. The class inherits two unrelated defaults with the same signature, and the compiler refuses to choose."
2 · Trace the mechanism "To fix it I override the method in the class. Inside the override I can call either parent's version explicitly with the interface name, dot super, dot the method."
3 · The rule that decides it "There are three rules, in order. A method from a class, including a superclass, beats any interface default. A more specific interface beats the one it extends. If neither applies, it is ambiguous and I must override."
4 · Variants that flip it "So it compiles without an override if a superclass already implements the method, or if one interface extends the other."
5 · The production version "Default methods exist so an interface can gain a method without breaking every implementer. They carry behaviour, not state, so Java still has no multiple inheritance of fields, and this conflict is the only diamond you can get."
Close "Compile error, explicit override, class beats interface, specific beats general."

stages.name: Predict it out loud
stages.html:
error: types Flyer and Swimmer are incompatible;
  class Duck inherits unrelated defaults for move() from types Flyer and Swimmer

The decision is made at compile time. There is no runtime ordering to rely on.

stages.name: Trace the mechanism
stages.html:
Prove it — the resolved version (JDK 25). Remove the override and it no longer compiles:

class Demo {
    interface Flyer { default String move() { return "fly"; } }
    interface Swimmer { default String move() { return "swim"; } }
    static class Duck implements Flyer, Swimmer {
        @Override public String move() {                      // without this override: compile error
            return Flyer.super.move() + " and " + Swimmer.super.move();
        }
    }
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        System.out.println(new Duck().move());
    }
}
// → fly and swim
Syntax Meaning
Flyer.super.move() call the default from the directly implemented interface Flyer
plain super.move() the superclass version, not an interface

stages.name: The rule that decides it
stages.html:
# Rule Example
1 a class method wins over an interface default a superclass's move() beats both defaults
2 the most specific interface wins if Swimmer extends Flyer, Swimmer.move() wins
3 otherwise: ambiguous, override required two unrelated interfaces

stages.name: Variants that flip it
stages.html:
Variant Result
two unrelated interfaces, same default compile error
a superclass defines move() compiles: the class method wins
Swimmer extends Flyer and overrides move() compiles: Swimmer wins
one interface declares it abstract, the other gives a default compile error: the other default does not satisfy the abstract method, so the class must override
same name, different parameter types compiles: they are overloads, not a conflict

stages.name: The production version
stages.html:
Purpose Example
evolve an interface without breaking implementers Collection.stream(), Iterable.forEach() added in Java 8
optional behaviour with a sensible fallback Comparator.reversed()
Interface defaults Abstract class
behaviour only: no instance fields can hold state and constructors
a class can implement many a class extends one

Where it bites: upgrading a library that adds a default method to an interface you implement alongside another with the same signature. The build breaks, which is the safe outcome.

followUps.question: Why doesn't Java just pick one?
followUps.html:
Because any automatic choice would change behaviour silently when a library adds a default.

Design Effect
pick by declaration order reordering implements changes behaviour
compile error the author decides, visibly

followUps.question: "The first interface in the implements list wins."
followUps.html:
Order in the list has no effect.

implements Flyer, Swimmer and implements Swimmer, Flyer ─▶ the same compile error

followUps.question: Can a default method override equals or hashCode?
followUps.html:
No. An interface can't provide defaults for Object's methods.

  • Rule 1 would make it useless: the class's inherited Object method always wins.
  • The compiler rejects it outright.

followUps.question: Is this the diamond problem?
followUps.html:
A limited form of it: behaviour only.

Diamond with state (C++) Java defaults
two copies of a field, or virtual inheritance no fields in interfaces, so only method choice is ambiguous

followUps.question: When would you avoid default methods?
followUps.html:
When the default would be wrong for many implementers.

  • A default that throws UnsupportedOperationException hides a missing implementation until run time.
  • Core behaviour belongs in an abstract method, so the compiler forces it.

dontSay: "The first interface wins."
"It throws at run time."
"Java now has multiple inheritance" — of behaviour, not of state.

java-spring-q7.testing: whether you know where in the lifecycle the proxy is created, because that explains self-invocation and init-time surprises.
java-spring-q7.trap: reciting callbacks without saying that proxying happens after initialisation.
java-spring-q7.spoken:
Beat Say
1 · The one-line claim "A bean goes from definition to instance to initialised object to, often, a proxy; and the proxy is created in the last post-processing step."
2 · The steps in order "First, bean-factory post-processors can change the definitions, before anything is created. Then, per bean: instantiate through the constructor, inject dependencies, call the aware callbacks, run post-processors' before-initialisation hook, run init callbacks such as at-PostConstruct, then run the after-initialisation hook. On shutdown, at-PreDestroy runs for singletons."
3 · Prove it "The after-initialisation hook is where AOP wraps the bean. So what the container stores and hands to others is the proxy, while at-PostConstruct ran earlier, on the raw object."
4 · What it costs or breaks "That ordering explains three things. A call on 'this' bypasses the proxy. A transactional method called from at-PostConstruct runs without a transaction. And prototypes never get their destroy callbacks, because the container doesn't track them."
5 · So what for the system "So I keep init methods simple, start real work on the application-ready event, and reason about every annotation as 'does this call go through the proxy?'"
Close "Instantiate, inject, initialise, then proxy: the order is the explanation."

stages.name: The one-line claim
stages.html:
The lifecycle:definitioninstantiateinjectawarepost-process beforeinitpost-process after = proxyin usedestroy
Phase Acts on
container startup bean definitions
per bean the instance
shutdown singleton instances

stages.name: The steps in order
stages.html:
# Step Hook or annotation Notes
0 change definitions BeanFactoryPostProcessor runs once, before any bean exists: property placeholders, configuration-class processing
1 instantiate constructor constructor injection happens here
2 populate field and setter injection @Autowired, @Value
3 aware callbacks BeanNameAware, ApplicationContextAware the bean learns about its container
4 before init BeanPostProcessor.postProcessBeforeInitialization @PostConstruct is itself processed here
5 init @PostConstruct, then afterPropertiesSet, then a custom init method dependencies are set; proxy not yet applied
6 after init BeanPostProcessor.postProcessAfterInitialization AOP proxies are created here
7 ready — singleton stored; this object is what others receive
8 destroy @PreDestroy, DisposableBean.destroy singletons only

stages.claim: what others receive is the proxy
stages.html:
Call Path Advice runs?
another bean calls service.save() caller → proxy → raw bean yes
this.save() inside the bean raw bean → raw bean no
save() called from @PostConstruct raw bean, proxy doesn't exist yet no

stages.name: What it costs or breaks
stages.html:
Surprise Cause in the lifecycle Fix
@Transactional ignored on an internal call this is the raw bean call through another bean, or use TransactionTemplate
no transaction or cache in @PostConstruct init runs before the proxy exists do the work on ApplicationReadyEvent, or from another bean
prototype @PreDestroy never runs the container doesn't keep prototypes release resources yourself
a field is null in the constructor field injection happens after construction constructor injection
a BeanPostProcessor isn't post-processed itself post-processors are created early keep them free of dependencies on ordinary beans

stages.html:
Work Put it in
validate configuration, build an immutable structure constructor or @PostConstruct
anything needing transactions, caches or other proxied behaviour ApplicationReadyEvent listener or ApplicationRunner
release pools, flush buffers @PreDestroy on a singleton
register definitions programmatically a BeanFactoryPostProcessor or an import registrar

Thread-safety: singleton initialisation is done once under the container's lock; after that the bean is shared, so its state must be safe for concurrent use.

followUps.html:
One edits the recipe, the other edits the dish.

BeanFactoryPostProcessor BeanPostProcessor
Works on bean definitions bean instances
Runs once, before instantiation around each bean's initialisation
Example property placeholder resolution AOP auto-proxy creator

followUps.question: "The proxy is created when the bean is instantiated."
followUps.html:
It is created after initialisation, around an already built bean.

instantiateinjectinitthen wrap

The exception is early proxy exposure to break a circular reference, which is one more reason to avoid cycles.

followUps.question: What is the order of the three init mechanisms?
followUps.html:
Annotation, then interface, then configured method.

@PostConstructInitializingBean.afterPropertiesSet()custom initMethod

Destruction mirrors it: @PreDestroy, DisposableBean.destroy(), custom destroy method.

followUps.question: When are singletons created?
followUps.html:
Eagerly at startup by default.

Mode Created Trade
eager (default) at context refresh wiring errors surface at startup
@Lazy or global lazy init on first use faster startup, errors appear later

followUps.question: How does this knowledge help during an incident?
followUps.html:
It turns "the annotation isn't working" into a checklist.

  • Is the object a bean, or was it created with new?
  • Does the call go through the proxy, or through this?
  • Was it called during init, before the proxy existed?
  • Is the method public and non-final?

dontSay: A list of callbacks with no mention of proxies.
"@PostConstruct runs after everything is ready" — not after proxying.
"Destroy callbacks always run."

java-spring-q8.testing: whether you understand @Transactional as proxy-based advice, and know the second silent failure: checked exceptions don't roll back by default.
java-spring-q8.trap: answering "yes, it's annotated", or stopping at self-invocation without the rollback rule.
java-spring-q8.spoken:
Beat Say
1 · Predict it out loud "No. The inner method runs, but without the transactional behaviour its annotation asks for."
2 · Trace the mechanism "At-Transactional is implemented by a proxy that wraps the bean. A call from outside goes to the proxy, which opens the transaction and then calls the real method. A call from inside the class goes through 'this', straight to the real object, so the proxy and its advice are never involved."
3 · The rule that decides it "The rule: advice runs only when the call passes through the proxy. The same applies to at-Async, at-Cacheable and at-Retryable."
4 · Variants that flip it "It works if I move the method to another bean, inject the bean into itself and call through that reference, use TransactionTemplate, or use AspectJ weaving. It also silently fails on private methods, and on final methods with class-based proxies."
5 · The production version "The second half is rollback. By default the transaction rolls back on unchecked exceptions only. A checked exception commits, unless I declare rollbackFor. Both failures are silent, so I test them: an integration test that asserts the data really rolled back."
Close "Through the proxy or it doesn't happen, and checked exceptions commit unless told otherwise."

stages.name: Predict it out loud
stages.claim: it runs, without a transaction of its own
stages.html:
@Service
class OrderService {
    public void placeOrder(Order o) {            // not transactional
        validate(o);
        saveOrder(o);                            // same as this.saveOrder(o): bypasses the proxy
    }
    @Transactional
    public void saveOrder(Order o) { /* two inserts that must be atomic */ }
}
Caller Transaction around saveOrder?
another bean calls orderService.saveOrder(o) yes
placeOrder calls saveOrder(o) no: each repository call commits by itself

stages.name: Trace the mechanism
stages.claim: the call never reaches the proxy
stages.html:
Prove it — a JDK dynamic proxy playing the role of Spring's transactional proxy (JDK 25):

import java.lang.reflect.Proxy;
class Demo {
    interface OrderService { void placeOrder(); void saveAudit(); }
    static class OrderServiceImpl implements OrderService {
        public void placeOrder() { System.out.println("  placeOrder body"); this.saveAudit(); }   // self-invocation
        public void saveAudit() { System.out.println("  saveAudit body"); }
    }
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        OrderService target = new OrderServiceImpl();
        OrderService proxy = (OrderService) Proxy.newProxyInstance(Demo.class.getClassLoader(),
            new Class<?>[]{OrderService.class}, (p, method, a) -> {
                System.out.println("TX begin for " + method.getName());
                Object r = method.invoke(target, a);
                System.out.println("TX commit for " + method.getName());
                return r; });
        proxy.placeOrder();        // advice runs once: the inner call never reaches the proxy
        proxy.saveAudit();         // called through the proxy: advice runs
    }
}
// → TX begin for placeOrder
// →   placeOrder body
// →   saveAudit body
// → TX commit for placeOrder
// → TX begin for saveAudit
// →   saveAudit body
// → TX commit for saveAudit
Output Meaning
one TX begin for placeOrder, then both bodies the inner saveAudit call got no advice
TX begin for saveAudit only on the direct proxy call advice runs when the call enters through the proxy
External call:callerproxybegintarget methodcommit or roll back
Internal call:target methodthis.other()target method (proxy not involved)

stages.name: The rule that decides it
stages.claim: through the proxy, or not at all
stages.html:
Annotation Same rule?
@Transactional yes
@Async yes: an internal call runs synchronously
@Cacheable, @CacheEvict yes: no caching on internal calls
@Retryable, method security (@PreAuthorize) yes

All of them are proxy-based advice applied in the after-initialisation step of the bean lifecycle.

stages.name: Variants that flip it
stages.html:
Variant Works? Note
move the method to another bean yes the cleanest fix: it usually reveals a missing class
TransactionTemplate around the code yes explicit, no proxy involved
self-injection (inject the bean's own proxy, call through it) yes works; reads oddly
AspectJ weaving yes advice is woven into the class itself
@Transactional on a private method no proxies can't intercept it
final method or class, with a class-based proxy no it can't be overridden
non-public method depends on version and proxy type: verify public is the safe choice
object created with new no it isn't a bean

stages.name: The production version
stages.html:
Exception thrown Default outcome
unchecked (RuntimeException, Error) roll back
checked (IOException, a custom checked exception) commit
checked, with rollbackFor = Exception.class roll back
caught and swallowed inside the method commit: the proxy never sees it

Example: placeOrder writes the order row and then the payment row. The payment insert fails. With self-invocation there was no surrounding transaction, so the order row stays: an order without a payment.

Guards:

  • An integration test that forces the failure and asserts both rows are absent.
  • A static-analysis or review rule for @Transactional on private methods and for internal calls to annotated methods.
  • Put @Transactional on the public entry method of the use case, not on helpers.

followUps.question: Why does Spring use proxies for this at all?
followUps.html:
So cross-cutting behaviour is added without changing or recompiling your classes.

Proxy-based AOP AspectJ weaving
no build step; works on beans only; public method calls from outside modifies bytecode; works on any call, including internal ones

followUps.question: "It's annotated, so it's transactional."
followUps.html:
The annotation is metadata; the proxy is the behaviour.

Annotated and… Transactional?
called through the proxy, public method yes
called through this, or private, or on a non-bean no

followUps.question: The outer method is @Transactional and calls an inner REQUIRES_NEW method in the same class.
followUps.html:
The inner method joins the outer transaction; REQUIRES_NEW is ignored.

  • The outer transaction was opened by the proxy.
  • The inner call goes through this, so its own annotation is never read.
  • An audit row meant to survive a rollback will roll back with everything else.

followUps.question: Is self-injection acceptable?
followUps.html:
It works, and it usually signals that the method belongs in another bean.

@Lazy @Autowired private OrderService self;     // the proxy
self.saveOrder(o);                               // now passes through advice

followUps.question: How do you catch this class of bug before production?
followUps.html:
By testing behaviour, since nothing throws.

  • Rollback test: force an exception, assert the database state.
  • Architecture test (for example with ArchUnit): no calls from a class to its own proxied-annotation methods.
  • Review habit: every @Transactional, @Async, @Cacheable gets the question "who calls this, and through what?"

dontSay: "Yes, because the method has the annotation."
"Make the method private and annotate it."
"Any exception rolls back."

java-spring-q9.testing: whether you know the two proxy kinds, the default in Spring Boot, and what each cannot intercept.
java-spring-q9.trap: a final service class, and hours lost wondering why it isn't transactional.
java-spring-q9.spoken:
Beat Say
1 · The one-line claim "Spring AOP wraps a bean in a proxy. There are two kinds: a JDK dynamic proxy, which implements the bean's interfaces, and a CGLIB proxy, which is a generated subclass of the bean's class."
2 · How it works "Plain Spring Framework uses a JDK proxy when the bean has an interface and CGLIB when it doesn't. Spring Boot sets proxy-target-class to true, so in a Boot application the default is CGLIB for everything."
3 · Prove it "A JDK proxy is an instance of the interface but not of the implementation class. So injecting by the concrete class fails with an interface proxy, and works with a subclass proxy. That is one reason Boot chose CGLIB."
4 · What it costs or breaks "A subclass proxy can't override final or private methods and can't subclass a final class. So advice on those is silently missing, or the application fails to start. And with both kinds, a call on 'this' bypasses the proxy."
5 · So what for the system "So service classes and their advised methods stay non-final and public. In Kotlin that means the all-open plugin. And if I need advice on internal calls, I restructure, or use AspectJ weaving."
Close "Interface proxy or subclass proxy; Boot defaults to subclass; final and private are invisible to it."

stages.name: The one-line claim
stages.claim: two ways to wrap a bean
stages.html:
JDK dynamic proxy CGLIB proxy
Is a class implementing the bean's interfaces a generated subclass of the bean's class
Needs at least one interface a non-final class
Injectable as the interface only the interface or the concrete class
Can't intercept methods not on the interface final and private methods

stages.name: How it works
stages.html:
Setting Bean has an interface Bean has no interface
Spring Framework default (proxyTargetClass = false) JDK proxy CGLIB
Spring Boot default (spring.aop.proxy-target-class=true, since Boot 2.0) CGLIB CGLIB
When the proxy is made:bean initialisedauto-proxy creator checks whether any advice appliesif yes, wrapthe proxy is what gets injected

stages.name: Prove it
stages.claim: what an interface proxy is and isn't
stages.html:
Prove it — JDK 25:

import java.lang.reflect.Proxy;
class Demo {
    interface Greeter { String hi(); }
    static class GreeterImpl implements Greeter { public String hi() { return "hi"; } }
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        Greeter target = new GreeterImpl();
        Greeter proxy = (Greeter) Proxy.newProxyInstance(Demo.class.getClassLoader(),
            new Class<?>[]{Greeter.class}, (p, m, a) -> "[advice] " + m.invoke(target, a));
        System.out.println(proxy.hi());
        System.out.println(proxy instanceof Greeter);            // the interface: yes
        System.out.println(proxy instanceof GreeterImpl);        // the concrete class: no
        System.out.println(Proxy.isProxyClass(proxy.getClass()));
    }
}
// → [advice] hi
// → true
// → false
// → true
Check Result Consequence
proxy instanceof Greeter true inject by interface: works
proxy instanceof GreeterImpl false inject by concrete class: no matching bean

With a CGLIB proxy the second line would be true, because the proxy extends the class.

stages.name: What it costs or breaks
stages.html:
Code With CGLIB Symptom
final class can't be subclassed startup failure when advice applies
final method not overridden the call runs on the proxy object without advice, and may see uninitialised fields
private method not overridden advice silently absent
call through this never reaches the proxy advice silently absent (both proxy kinds)
constructor logic runs for the target; the proxy instance is created without calling it don't rely on constructor side effects of the proxy

stages.name: So what for the system
stages.html:
Rule Why
advised methods are public and non-final so the proxy can intercept them
bean classes are non-final (Kotlin: kotlin-spring / all-open) so they can be subclassed
cross-cutting annotations on the entry method of a use case so the call comes from outside
for advice on internal calls: another bean, or AspectJ proxies can't see them

Debugging: AopUtils.isAopProxy(bean) and the class name ($$SpringCGLIB$$ or $Proxy) tell you which kind you have.

followUps.question: Why did Boot switch the default to CGLIB?
followUps.html:
To remove a class of injection failures.

With JDK proxies With CGLIB
injecting the concrete class fails with a confusing "bean not of required type" injection by class or interface both work

followUps.question: "CGLIB proxies are much slower."
followUps.html:
Not in any way that matters next to a database call.

  • Both add a small per-call overhead.
  • The advised operation (a transaction, a cache lookup) costs far more.
  • Choose on capability, not on proxy speed.

followUps.question: A final method on a CGLIB-proxied bean reads a field and gets null.
followUps.html:
It ran on the proxy instance, whose fields were never initialised.

call proxy.finalMethod()not overriddenexecutes on the proxy objectits own fields are emptynull

A non-final method would have been delegated to the real target.

followUps.question: How does AspectJ differ?
followUps.html:
It changes the class itself instead of wrapping it.

Spring AOP (proxies) AspectJ weaving
When at run time, per bean at compile time or class-load time
Internal calls not intercepted intercepted
Setup none a weaver in the build or an agent

followUps.question: What does this mean for native images and AOT?
followUps.html:
Proxies must be known at build time.

  • Spring's AOT processing generates proxy classes ahead of time.
  • Anything creating proxies dynamically at run time needs explicit hints.
  • It is one more reason to keep proxy use conventional.

dontSay: "Spring always uses JDK proxies for interfaces" — not in Boot.
"Mark services final for safety."
"The proxy is my object" — it wraps or extends it.

java-spring-q10.testing: whether you can replace "magic" with: a list of candidate configurations, each guarded by conditions, that back off when you define your own bean.

2 · How it works "At-SpringBootApplication includes at-EnableAutoConfiguration. That loads candidate class names from a file in each jar: AutoConfiguration dot imports since Boot 2.7, spring dot factories before. Each candidate carries conditions: on class, on missing bean, on property, on web application."
3 · Prove it "Take the data source. If a JDBC driver and the pool library are on the classpath, and I haven't defined a DataSource bean, Boot creates one from the spring-datasource properties. If I define my own, the on-missing-bean condition fails and Boot backs off."
4 · What it costs or breaks "The classpath is an input. Add a dependency and behaviour changes: a new starter can switch on a whole subsystem. And ordering matters: my beans are registered before auto-configurations are evaluated."
5 · So what for the system "When something is or isn't configured, I read the conditions report: run with debug, or use the actuator conditions endpoint. It lists every candidate with the condition that matched or failed."

java-spring-q11.testing: whether you separate visibility and ordering from atomicity, and can show the lost update.
java-spring-q11.spoken:
Beat Say
1 · The one-line claim "Volatile guarantees visibility and ordering. It does not guarantee atomicity."
2 · How it works "A write to a volatile field happens-before every later read of it. So a reader always sees the latest write, and everything the writer did before that write is visible too. The compiler and CPU may not reorder across it."
3 · Prove it "What it doesn't cover is compound operations. Count plus-plus is a read, an add and a write. Two threads can both read the same value and both write back the same result. In a run with four threads doing a million increments each, the volatile counter loses updates; the atomic one ends at exactly four million."
4 · What it costs or breaks "A volatile read or write is cheaper than a lock but not free, and using it where atomicity is needed gives a bug that only shows under load."
5 · So what for the system "So I use volatile for flags and for publishing an immutable reference, such as a config snapshot that is replaced whole. For counters I use AtomicLong or LongAdder; for invariants over several fields, a lock."
Close "Volatile makes a write visible; it doesn't make read-modify-write atomic."

stages.name: The one-line claim
stages.html:
Guarantee volatile synchronized / lock Atomic*
visibility of the latest write yes yes yes
ordering (happens-before) yes yes yes
atomic read-modify-write no yes yes (CAS)
mutual exclusion over several fields no yes no

stages.name: How it works
stages.html:
Thread A:  x = 42;  ready = true;      ← ready is volatile
Thread B:  if (ready) use(x);          ← guaranteed to see x == 42

rule: a write to a volatile field happens-before every subsequent read of that field,
      and happens-before is transitive, so earlier writes by A are visible too
Without volatile With volatile
B may never see ready == true (the JIT can hoist the read out of a loop) B sees it on its next read
B may see ready but a stale x B sees x == 42

Other happens-before edges: unlocking a monitor before the next lock of it, Thread.start() before the thread's first action, a thread's last action before join() returns, final-field writes before the constructor's end is observed.

stages.name: Prove it
stages.html:
Prove it — 4 threads × 1,000,000 increments (JDK 25):

import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicInteger;
class Demo {
    static volatile int plain = 0;
    static final AtomicInteger atomic = new AtomicInteger();
    public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception {
        Thread[] ts = new Thread[4];
        for (int i = 0; i < 4; i++) {
            ts[i] = new Thread(() -> { for (int j = 0; j < 1_000_000; j++) { plain++; atomic.incrementAndGet(); } });
            ts[i].start();
        }
        for (Thread t : ts) t.join();
        System.out.println("atomic: " + atomic.get());
        System.out.println("volatile lost updates: " + (plain < 4_000_000));
    }
}
// → atomic: 4000000
// → volatile lost updates: true
plain++ is three steps: read plainadd 1write plain
Step Thread A Thread B plain
1 reads 5 5
2 reads 5 5
3 writes 6 6
4 writes 6 6: one increment lost

Each individual read and write was visible. The interleaving is the problem.

stages.name: What it costs or breaks
stages.html:
Use Verdict
a stop flag: one writer, many readers correct
publishing an immutable snapshot by replacing the reference correct
the instance field in double-checked locking required: without it a reader can see a partly constructed object
a counter, count++ broken
check-then-act: if (x == null) x = create() broken
two fields that must change together broken: each is visible, the pair isn't atomic

stages.name: So what for the system
stages.html:
Need Tool
a flag or a published reference volatile
a counter under moderate contention AtomicLong
a hot metrics counter LongAdder
an invariant across several fields synchronized or a lock
a lazily created singleton the holder-class idiom, or an enum

Example: feature-flag configuration reloaded every minute. Build a new immutable map, assign it to a volatile field. Readers see either the old or the new map, never a half-updated one.

followUps.question: Why does double-checked locking need volatile?
followUps.html:
Because the reference can be published before the constructor has finished.

Without it:allocateassign referencerun constructor
Another thread:sees non-nulluses a half-built object

volatile forbids that reordering.

followUps.question: "I made the counter volatile, so it's thread-safe."
followUps.html:
Visible, not atomic.

Fix When
AtomicLong.incrementAndGet() general
LongAdder.increment() very hot counters, read rarely

followUps.question: Is a volatile reference to a mutable object safe?
followUps.html:
Only the reference is volatile, not the object's fields.

Operation Covered?
replacing the reference yes
mutating the object it points to no

Hence: publish immutable objects through it.

followUps.question: long and double without volatile?
followUps.html:
The language allows a non-volatile 64-bit write to be split into two 32-bit writes.

  • volatile long writes are atomic.
  • On mainstream 64-bit JVMs tearing isn't observed in practice, but the specification permits it.

followUps.question: How do these bugs show up in production?
followUps.html:
As rare, load-dependent wrong numbers, never as an exception.

  • Metrics that undercount at peak.
  • A worker that never stops because it can't see the flag.
  • Found by code review and stress tests (for example jcstress), not by unit tests.

dontSay: "volatile makes it thread-safe."
"volatile is a lightweight lock."
"It flushes the CPU cache" — describe it by the happens-before guarantee.

java-spring-q12.testing: whether you know the Java 8 design (volatile reads, CAS, per-bin locks) and that single operations being safe doesn't make a sequence of them safe.
java-spring-q12.spoken:
Beat Say
1 · The one-line claim "Reads don't lock because the table and its nodes are read through volatile semantics, so a reader always sees a consistent, published state. Writers lock only one bucket."
2 · How it works "Since Java 8 there are no segments. An insert into an empty bucket is a compare-and-swap. An insert into a non-empty bucket synchronises on that bucket's first node. A node's value and next pointer are volatile, so a concurrent reader walking the chain sees either the old or the new link, never a broken one. Resizing is cooperative: writers that meet a resize help move buckets."
3 · Prove it "Four threads doing a hundred thousand merges each end at exactly four hundred thousand. The same threads doing get-then-put on the same map lose updates, although every single call was thread-safe."
4 · What it costs or breaks "The costs: size is an estimate while writes are in flight, iterators are weakly consistent, and nulls aren't allowed as keys or values."
5 · So what for the system "So compound actions go through the atomic methods: putIfAbsent, computeIfAbsent, compute, merge. And I keep the functions passed to them short, since they run while the bucket is locked."
Close "Volatile reads, per-bucket writes, and atomic methods for anything that is more than one step."

stages.name: The one-line claim
stages.html:
Operation Synchronisation
get none: volatile reads of the table slot and node fields
put into an empty bin one compare-and-swap
put into an occupied bin synchronized on that bin's head node
resize cooperative transfer, bin by bin
size, mappingCount sum of striped counter cells

stages.name: How it works
stages.html:
put(k, v):spread hashbin empty? CAS the node inelse lock the bin headupdate or appendtreeify at 8add to the counter
Design choice Why
no segments (they were removed in Java 8) locking is per bin, so contention is far finer
volatile val and next in each node a reader sees a fully linked chain at every moment
forwarding nodes during resize a reader that hits a moved bin is sent to the new table
counter cells like LongAdder counting doesn't become a single contended variable
null keys and values forbidden get returning null must mean "absent", unambiguously

stages.name: Prove it
stages.html:
Prove it — 4 threads × 100,000 updates of one key (JDK 25):

import java.util.concurrent.*;
class Demo {
    public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception {
        ConcurrentHashMap<String, Integer> safe = new ConcurrentHashMap<>(), racy = new ConcurrentHashMap<>();
        Runnable work = () -> {
            for (int i = 0; i < 100_000; i++) {
                safe.merge("hits", 1, Integer::sum);                              // atomic per key
                Integer v = racy.get("hits"); racy.put("hits", v == null ? 1 : v + 1);   // get-then-put
            }
        };
        Thread[] ts = new Thread[4];
        for (int i = 0; i < 4; i++) { ts[i] = new Thread(work); ts[i].start(); }
        for (Thread t : ts) t.join();
        System.out.println("merge: " + safe.get("hits"));
        System.out.println("get-then-put lost updates: " + (racy.get("hits") < 400_000));
    }
}
// → merge: 400000
// → get-then-put lost updates: true
Code Result Why
merge("hits", 1, Integer::sum) exactly 400,000 read, add and write happen under the bin lock
get then put fewer: updates lost another thread can write between the two calls

stages.name: What it costs or breaks
stages.html:
Property Behaviour Consequence
size() an estimate under concurrent writes don't use it for control flow
iteration weakly consistent: no exception, may miss or include concurrent changes not a snapshot
bulk reads (forEach, reduce) not atomic over the map totals can be off while writers run
nulls not allowed computeIfAbsent returning null means "don't insert"
a mapping function that is slow, or that updates the same map blocks the bin; recursive update can fail keep it short and side-effect free

stages.name: So what for the system
stages.html:
Intent Wrong Right
insert if absent if (!m.containsKey(k)) m.put(k, v) m.putIfAbsent(k, v)
create lazily if (m.get(k) == null) m.put(k, load()) m.computeIfAbsent(k, key -> load())
increment m.put(k, m.get(k) + 1) m.merge(k, 1, Integer::sum)
conditional update get, check, put m.compute(k, (key, v) -> …) or replace(k, old, new)

Thread-safety: each method is atomic for its key. Invariants across keys still need an external lock or a different design.

followUps.question: How was Java 7's version different?
followUps.html:
It locked segments, each a small hash table.

Java 7 Java 8+
Lock granularity one of 16 segments by default one bin
Concurrency level fixed at construction grows with the table

followUps.question: "ConcurrentHashMap makes my code thread-safe."
followUps.html:
It makes each call thread-safe, not your sequence of calls.

Code Safe?
one call to put, get, merge yes
get … decide … put no

followUps.question: computeIfAbsent is used as a cache loader and the loader is slow.
followUps.html:
Other writers to that bin wait, and a loader that touches the same map can break.

  • Load outside, then putIfAbsent, accepting an occasional duplicate load.
  • Or store a CompletableFuture as the value so only the first caller loads.
  • Or use a cache library built for it.

followUps.question: Collections.synchronizedMap or ConcurrentHashMap?
followUps.html:
ConcurrentHashMap, almost always.

synchronizedMap ConcurrentHashMap
Locking one lock for every operation per bin; reads lock-free
Iteration caller must hold the lock weakly consistent, no lock

followUps.question: Where does it fall short as a cache?
followUps.html:
It has no eviction, expiry or size bound.

Need Use
bounded size, expiry, statistics a cache library such as Caffeine
a simple registry that never shrinks ConcurrentHashMap

An unbounded map used as a cache is one of the usual sources of a slow heap leak.

dontSay: "It locks segments" — that was Java 7.
"It's fully consistent" — size and iteration are not.
"containsKey then put is fine, the map is concurrent."

java-spring-q13.testing: whether you check independence first, parallelise on a dedicated executor, and add per-call timeouts and partial-failure handling.
java-spring-q13.trap: parallelising calls that depend on each other, or running them on the shared common pool.
java-spring-q13.spoken:
Beat Say
1 · Name it "If the three calls are independent, the latency is their sum when it could be their maximum. That is the problem to fix."
2 · Rule out the fakes "First I'd check that they really are independent: does call two need the result of call one? And whether one call dominates, in which case parallelism helps little and that call is the real work."
3 · Confirm with evidence "A trace of the request shows it: three spans laid end to end, a hundred, two hundred and three hundred milliseconds, six hundred in total."
4 · Fix by experiment "The fix is to start all three with CompletableFuture supplyAsync on a dedicated executor, wait for all of them, and combine. Total time becomes about three hundred. Each call gets its own timeout and its own fallback, so one slow dependency can't define my response time."
5 · Validate "I'd validate at p95 under load, not on one request, and watch the executor's queue."
6 · Productionise "In production the executor is bounded and named, trace context is propagated into the tasks, and the fan-out sits behind a bulkhead. On a current JDK, virtual threads let me write it as plain blocking code."
Close "Independent calls in parallel on my own pool: the slowest one, not the sum, and each with a timeout."

stages.name: Name it
stages.claim: sum when it could be max
stages.html:
sequential:  user 100 ms + orders 200 ms + offers 300 ms = 600 ms
parallel:    max(100, 200, 300)                         = 300 ms
Sequential:call Awaitcall Bwaitcall Cwaitcombine
Parallel:start A, B, C togetherwait for allcombine

stages.name: Rule out the fakes
stages.html:
Check If true
B needs A's result they stay in sequence: use thenCompose, parallelise only the rest
one call is 90% of the time fix or cache that call; parallelism gains little
the calls hit the same overloaded backend parallel calls add load to the thing that is slow
a call isn't needed for most requests make it lazy or optional
the same data is fetched on every request cache it

stages.name: Confirm with evidence
stages.html:
Observation Likely cause Next action
three client spans in sequence, no overlap independent calls made serially run them concurrently
one span far longer than the others a slow dependency timeout, fallback, and look at that service
long gaps between spans time in my own code or waiting for a thread profile; check pool saturation
spans overlap already they are parallel; the cost is elsewhere look at the slowest span

stages.name: Fix by experiment
stages.html:
Prove it — JDK 25:

import java.util.concurrent.*;
class Demo {
    static String call(String name, int ms) { try { Thread.sleep(ms); } catch (InterruptedException e) { } return name; }
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        ExecutorService pool = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(3);                  // a dedicated executor
        long t0 = System.nanoTime();
        var user = CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> call("user", 100), pool);
        var orders = CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> call("orders", 200), pool);
        var offers = CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> call("offers", 300), pool)
            .completeOnTimeout("no-offers", 250, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS);         // per-call timeout with a fallback
        CompletableFuture.allOf(user, orders, offers).join();
        long ms = (System.nanoTime() - t0) / 1_000_000;
        System.out.println(user.join() + ", " + orders.join() + ", " + offers.join());
        System.out.println("sequential would be 600 ms; took under 400 ms: " + (ms < 400));
        pool.shutdownNow();
    }
}
// → user, orders, no-offers
// → sequential would be 600 ms; took under 400 ms: true
Element Why
supplyAsync(task, pool) with my own executor the default is the common ForkJoinPool: small, shared by the whole JVM, wrong for blocking I/O
allOf(…).join() wait for all, then read each result
completeOnTimeout / orTimeout per-call deadline; here offers was replaced by a fallback at 250 ms
exceptionally / handle per branch a failed optional call degrades the response instead of failing it

stages.name: Validate
stages.html:
Metric Before After
p95 endpoint latency measure measure
executor active threads and queue depth — measure: must not saturate
downstream error and timeout rate measure measure
share of responses served with a fallback — measure

Three times the concurrent calls reach the downstream services; confirm they can take it.

stages.name: Productionise
stages.html:
Concern Practice
executor bounded pool and queue, named threads, one per downstream group (bulkhead)
timeouts on the HTTP client and on the future
context trace IDs, MDC and security context don't cross threads by themselves: use a context-propagating executor
failure policy decide per call: required (fail the request) or optional (fallback)
cancellation when one required call fails, cancel the others
JDK 21+ virtual threads: one blocking call per virtual thread, joined with invokeAll or structured concurrency where available

Thread-safety: the three tasks must not share mutable state; each returns its own result.

followUps.question: Why not the default executor?
followUps.html:
The common pool is sized for CPU work and shared by everyone.

Common ForkJoinPool Dedicated executor
Size about cores − 1 chosen for I/O wait
Shared with parallel streams, other futures nobody
Blocking I/O in it starves unrelated code contained

followUps.question: "Just add .parallel() or make everything async."
followUps.html:
Parallelism on dependent calls gives wrong results, and on the shared pool gives outages.

  • Check independence first.
  • Give blocking work its own pool.
  • Keep dependent steps chained with thenCompose.

followUps.question: One of the three is required and it fails.
followUps.html:
Fail fast and cancel the rest.

Call On failure
required fail the request; cancel siblings
optional substitute a default; continue

followUps.question: thenCombine or allOf?
followUps.html:
thenCombine for two results with a typed merge; allOf for many.

user.thenCombine(orders, (u, o) -> new Page(u, o));     // two
CompletableFuture.allOf(a, b, c).thenApply(v -> merge(a.join(), b.join(), c.join()));   // many

followUps.question: When would you not fan out from this service at all?
followUps.html:
When the composition is needed by many clients, or the data can be precomputed.

Alternative When
a read model or cache built ahead of time the combined view changes rarely
an aggregation layer (BFF or gateway) several clients need the same composition

dontSay: "Make it async" without checking the calls are independent.
"Use supplyAsync" with no executor argument.
"It's three times faster" — it is the slowest call, plus overhead.

java-spring-q14.testing: whether you can name each component in order and, from that, say which layer can and can't handle a given concern.
java-spring-q14.trap: expecting @ControllerAdvice to catch an exception thrown in a servlet filter.
java-spring-q14.spoken:
Beat Say
1 · The one-line claim "A request passes through servlet filters, then one front controller, the DispatcherServlet, which finds the handler, invokes it through an adapter, and turns the return value into a response."
2 · The path in order "Filters run first, including the Spring Security chain. The DispatcherServlet asks its handler mappings for the controller method and its interceptors. Interceptors' pre-handle runs. The handler adapter resolves the method's arguments, binding and validating the body and parameters, and calls my method. The return value goes to a message converter, usually Jackson, which writes the body. Interceptors' post-handle and after-completion run on the way out."
3 · Prove it "For a post with a JSON body: the converter reads JSON into the at-RequestBody object, validation runs, the method returns a DTO, and the converter writes it back as JSON."
4 · What it costs or breaks "Exceptions thrown inside that dispatch are routed to exception resolvers, which is where at-ControllerAdvice lives. An exception in a filter never gets there, because filters are outside the DispatcherServlet."
5 · So what for the system "So I place each concern by layer: protocol and security in filters, handler-aware logic in interceptors, error mapping in controller advice."
Close "Filters, dispatcher, mapping, adapter, handler, converter, with advice on the error path inside the dispatcher only."

stages.name: The one-line claim
stages.html:
The path:filtersDispatcherServlethandler mappinginterceptorshandler adaptercontroller methodmessage converterresponse
Layer Owned by
filters the servlet container
everything after Spring MVC, inside DispatcherServlet

stages.name: The path in order
stages.html:
# Component Does
1 servlet filters encoding, CORS, security chain, logging; can wrap request and response
2 DispatcherServlet the single entry point for MVC
3 HandlerMapping URL, method and headers → controller method plus interceptor chain
4 HandlerInterceptor.preHandle handler-aware checks; can stop the request
5 HandlerAdapter resolves arguments (@PathVariable, @RequestParam, @RequestBody), runs validation
6 controller method your code
7 return-value handling @ResponseBody → HttpMessageConverter (Jackson) writes JSON
8 postHandle, afterCompletion interceptors on the way out

stages.name: Prove it
stages.html:
@PostMapping("/orders")
ResponseEntity<OrderDto> create(@Valid @RequestBody CreateOrder cmd) {
    return ResponseEntity.status(201).body(service.create(cmd));
}
Stage What happens to POST /orders with a JSON body
filters authenticated; request ID added
mapping matched to create by path and method
argument resolution Jackson converter reads JSON into CreateOrder
validation @Valid runs; a violation throws MethodArgumentNotValidException
invocation service.create(cmd)
return value converter chosen by the Accept header writes OrderDto as JSON, status 201

stages.name: What it costs or breaks
stages.html:
Exception thrown in Handled by @ControllerAdvice? Handled by
controller, service, argument binding, validation yes HandlerExceptionResolver chain → @ExceptionHandler
an interceptor yes the same chain
a servlet filter (including security filters) no the filter itself, the security entry point, or the container's error page

Other costs: reading the body is one-shot, so a filter that logs it must wrap the request; every interceptor and filter adds to each request's time.

stages.name: So what for the system
stages.html:
Concern Layer
authentication, CORS, compression, body wrapping filter
per-handler checks, timing, tenant resolution from annotations interceptor
mapping exceptions to HTTP problem responses @RestControllerAdvice
security errors (401, 403) AuthenticationEntryPoint, AccessDeniedHandler

followUps.question: How does Spring choose the response format?
followUps.html:
Content negotiation between the Accept header and the available converters.

Accept headerproducible types of the handlerfirst converter that can write the typebody

followUps.question: "@ControllerAdvice handles every exception in the app."
followUps.html:
Only those raised inside the DispatcherServlet's dispatch.

Raised in Reaches the advice
controller or anything it calls yes
a filter no

followUps.question: No handler matches the URL.
followUps.html:
The DispatcherServlet answers 404 itself; your interceptors for handlers don't run.

  • Filters still ran, since they are before dispatch.
  • To customise, handle NoHandlerFoundException / NoResourceFoundException in the advice.
