followUps.html:
During argument resolution, before your method is called.

Annotation Failure exception
@Valid @RequestBody MethodArgumentNotValidException
constraints on parameters HandlerMethodValidationException or ConstraintViolationException, by version

followUps.question: How does this change with async or streaming responses?
followUps.html:
The servlet thread is released and the response completes later on another thread.

Return type Effect
Callable, DeferredResult, CompletableFuture request thread freed; dispatch resumes when the result is ready
SseEmitter, ResponseBodyEmitter the response stays open for a stream

dontSay: "The controller receives the request" — a lot happens first.
"ControllerAdvice catches security errors."
"Interceptors and filters are the same thing."

java-spring-q15.testing: whether you know it is a chain of servlet filters in front of MVC, with a thread-bound security context, and method security by proxy.
java-spring-q15.trap: losing the security context when work moves to another thread.
java-spring-q15.spoken:
Beat Say
1 · The one-line claim "Spring Security is one servlet filter that delegates to an ordered chain of security filters, running before the request reaches the DispatcherServlet."
2 · How it works "An authentication filter extracts credentials, a bearer token for example, and asks the authentication manager to verify them. On success the result is stored in the SecurityContextHolder, which is thread-local by default. Later in the chain an authorisation filter checks the request against the configured rules. Method-level rules, such as at-PreAuthorize, are enforced by proxies around beans."
3 · Prove it "For a stateless JWT API: no session; each request carries the token; the filter verifies signature, expiry, issuer and audience against cached keys, and builds the authentication from the claims."
4 · What it costs or breaks "Two things bite. The context is bound to the thread, so an at-Async method or a task in my own executor doesn't see it unless I propagate it. And method security is proxy-based, so a call through 'this' skips the check."
5 · So what for the system "So URL rules are the outer guard, method security is the inner one on service entry points, context propagation is configured for every executor, and errors are handled by the entry point and access-denied handler, not by controller advice."
Close "A filter chain before MVC, a thread-bound context, and proxies for method rules."

stages.html:
Where it sits:servlet containerDelegatingFilterProxyFilterChainProxya SecurityFilterChain matched by requestDispatcherServlet
Piece Role
DelegatingFilterProxy a servlet filter that hands over to a Spring bean
FilterChainProxy (springSecurityFilterChain) picks the matching SecurityFilterChain

stages.html:
Step Component
extract credentials an authentication filter: bearer token, form login, basic
verify AuthenticationManager → an AuthenticationProvider
remember for this request SecurityContextHolder (thread-local by default)

@Bean
SecurityFilterChain api(HttpSecurity http) throws Exception {      // Spring Security 6.x style
    return http
        .securityMatcher("/api/**")
        .authorizeHttpRequests(a -> a.requestMatchers("/api/admin/**").hasRole("ADMIN").anyRequest().authenticated())
        .oauth2ResourceServer(o -> o.jwt(Customizer.withDefaults()))
        .sessionManagement(s -> s.sessionCreationPolicy(SessionCreationPolicy.STATELESS))
        .build();
}
Check on each token Why
signature against the issuer's keys (JWKS, cached) it was issued by who it claims
exp, nbf not expired, not used early
iss, aud meant for this API
scopes or roles → authorities input to authorisation

stages.name: What it costs or breaks
stages.html:
Failure Symptom Fix
context lost across threads @Async method sees no user; @PreAuthorize there denies or throws DelegatingSecurityContextExecutor, or the context-propagation support for your executor
self-invocation @PreAuthorize on an internal call is skipped put it on the bean's entry method; call through another bean
rule order a broad matcher placed first shadows a specific one most specific matchers first; anyRequest() last
errors from filters @ControllerAdvice never sees them customise the entry point and access-denied handler
CSRF disabled or enabled blindly either broken forms or an exposed session-based app disable only for stateless token APIs

stages.name: So what for the system
stages.html:
Layer Rule kind
URL (filter chain) coarse: which paths need which role or scope
method (@PreAuthorize) fine: this user may act on this resource
data row-level filters by tenant in queries

Thread-safety: the context is per thread by design. Anything that hops threads (async methods, parallel streams, reactive pipelines, message listeners) needs deliberate propagation.

Trust boundary: a token's claims are trusted only after signature and audience checks pass.

followUps.question: Authentication or authorisation: which component does which?
followUps.html:
Different filters, different questions.

Authentication Authorisation
Question who are you may you do this
Component authentication filter + AuthenticationManager AuthorizationFilter, method security
Failure 401 403

followUps.question: "The security context is available everywhere in the request."
followUps.html:
Everywhere on the request thread.

Where the code runs Context
the request thread present
@Async, your own executor, parallelStream absent unless propagated

followUps.question: How do you revoke a JWT before it expires?
followUps.html:
You can't with pure stateless validation, so you design around it.

  • Short-lived access tokens plus refresh tokens.
  • A deny list checked on each request, for the rare forced logout.
  • Opaque tokens with introspection when immediate revocation is required.

followUps.question: Why is CSRF protection off for token APIs?
followUps.html:
CSRF abuses credentials the browser attaches automatically, and a bearer header isn't one.

Credential Sent automatically by the browser CSRF risk
session cookie yes yes
Authorization header no no

followUps.question: How do you test that the rules are what you think?
followUps.html:
Slice tests that send requests as different principals.

  • MockMvc with security: anonymous → 401, wrong role → 403, right role → 200, per endpoint.
  • Method-security tests on services with a mocked user.
  • A default-deny rule (anyRequest().denyAll() or authenticated()) so a new endpoint is never open by accident.

dontSay: "Spring Security uses AOP" — URL security is filters; only method security is proxies.
"The user is in a ThreadLocal, so it's available in async code."
"Disable CSRF, it gets in the way."

java-spring-q16.testing: whether you choose by capability (timeout, interruption, fairness, conditions), not by a belief about speed.
java-spring-q16.spoken:
Beat Say
1 · Frame the axis "Both give mutual exclusion and both are reentrant. The difference is simplicity against capability."
2 · Where synchronized wins "Synchronized is built into the language. The lock is released automatically when the block exits, even on an exception, so I can't forget. For a short critical section it is the default."
3 · Where the lock wins "ReentrantLock offers what the keyword can't. tryLock with a timeout, so a thread can give up instead of waiting for ever. lockInterruptibly, so a waiting thread can be cancelled. An optional fairness policy. And several condition objects on one lock, for example 'not full' and 'not empty' on a bounded buffer."
4 · The deciding question "So I ask: do I need to bound the wait, cancel the wait, or wait on more than one condition? If not, synchronized."
5 · What I'd pick here "The price of the explicit lock is that I own the unlock: it must be in a finally block. Performance is comparable in ordinary use. With virtual threads, synchronized used to pin the carrier thread; that was fixed in JDK 24, so on older JDKs the lock is preferable around blocking calls."
Close "Synchronized by default; the explicit lock when I need timeout, interruption, fairness or multiple conditions."

stages.name: Frame the axis
stages.html:
synchronized ReentrantLock
Release automatic at block exit manual: unlock() in finally
Reentrant yes yes
Timed or non-blocking acquire no tryLock(), tryLock(timeout)
Interruptible wait no lockInterruptibly()
Fairness no optional (new ReentrantLock(true))
Conditions one wait set per monitor many Condition objects
Pick when a short, simple critical section you need one of the four capabilities

stages.name: Where synchronized wins
stages.html:
synchronized (accountLock) {      // released on normal exit and on exception
    balance -= amount;
}
Property Benefit
structured lock and unlock are one syntactic block
JVM-optimised cheap when uncontended
shows in thread dumps "waiting to lock" with the owner named

stages.name: Where the lock wins
stages.html:
Prove it — a thread that gives up after 100 ms (JDK 25):

import java.util.concurrent.TimeUnit;
import java.util.concurrent.locks.ReentrantLock;
class Demo {
    public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception {
        ReentrantLock lock = new ReentrantLock();
        lock.lock();                                           // main holds the lock
        Thread t = new Thread(() -> {
            try {
                boolean got = lock.tryLock(100, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS);     // give up instead of waiting for ever
                System.out.println("acquired within 100 ms: " + got);
                if (got) lock.unlock();
            } catch (InterruptedException e) { System.out.println("interrupted while waiting"); }
        });
        t.start(); t.join();
        try { System.out.println("held by main: " + lock.isHeldByCurrentThread()); }
        finally { lock.unlock(); }                             // always in finally
    }
}
// → acquired within 100 ms: false
// → held by main: true
Capability Use
tryLock(timeout) avoid deadlock by backing off; fail fast under contention
lockInterruptibly() a cancelled task stops waiting
fair lock prevents starvation, at a throughput cost
multiple Conditions wake only the waiters that can make progress
isLocked, getQueueLength diagnostics

stages.name: The deciding question
stages.html:
Need Choice
none of the four synchronized
bound or cancel the wait ReentrantLock
many readers, few writers ReentrantReadWriteLock, or StampedLock for optimistic reads
a single variable Atomic*: no lock
a map ConcurrentHashMap
blocking I/O inside the section, on virtual threads, before JDK 24 ReentrantLock, to avoid pinning

stages.name: What I'd pick here
stages.claim: and the price of the lock
stages.html:
lock.lock();
try {
    // critical section
} finally {
    lock.unlock();               // without this, one exception leaks the lock for ever
}
Risk with explicit locks Guard
forgotten or skipped unlock always try/finally, acquired before the try
unlocking a lock you don't hold check tryLock's result before the try
holding it across slow I/O keep sections short; copy data out, release, then call

Thread-safety: both are reentrant, so the same thread can re-acquire; neither protects state that is also touched without the lock.

followUps.question: What is AQS?
followUps.html:
The queueing framework underneath ReentrantLock and most of java.util.concurrent.

Part Role
an int state updated by CAS lock held or not, and the hold count
a FIFO queue of waiting threads parked until the state allows them

followUps.question: "ReentrantLock is faster, so prefer it."
followUps.html:
In ordinary use they perform alike; the choice is about features.

  • Uncontended: both are very cheap.
  • A fair lock is slower than either.
  • Measure before claiming a difference.

followUps.question: How does tryLock help against deadlock?
followUps.html:
A thread that can't get the second lock releases the first and retries.

lock AtryLock(B, timeout) failsunlock Aback off with jitterretry

The simpler cure remains a fixed global order for acquiring locks.

followUps.question: What changed with virtual threads?
followUps.html:
Blocking inside synchronized used to pin the carrier thread.

JDK synchronized + blocking call on a virtual thread
21–23 pins the carrier: can exhaust the small carrier pool
24+ no longer pins (JEP 491)

followUps.question: How do you find lock contention in production?
followUps.html:
Thread dumps and JFR.

  • Thread dumps: many threads BLOCKED on one monitor, with its owner.
  • JFR lock events: which locks, how long.
  • Then shorten the section, split the lock, or remove shared state.

dontSay: "ReentrantLock is faster."
"synchronized is deprecated in modern Java."
An explicit lock with no finally.

java-spring-q17.testing: whether you know that REQUIRES_NEW holds a second connection while the first is suspended, and that an inner REQUIRED rollback dooms the outer transaction.
java-spring-q17.trap: REQUIRES_NEW in a loop, exhausting the connection pool against itself.
java-spring-q17.spoken:
Beat Say
1 · Frame the axis "Propagation answers: when a transactional method is called and a transaction already exists, do I join it or start my own?"
2 · Where REQUIRED fits "Required, the default, joins the caller's transaction or starts one. Everything commits or rolls back together. The catch: if the inner method throws and marks the transaction rollback-only, the outer one can't commit even if it catches the exception."
3 · Where REQUIRES_NEW fits "Requires-new suspends the outer transaction and runs in a separate one, with its own connection, that commits or rolls back independently. The classic use is an audit record that must survive a business rollback."
4 · The deciding question "So I ask: must this work survive the caller's rollback? If not, required."
5 · What I'd pick here "It bites on resources. During requires-new the thread holds two connections. With a pool of ten and ten concurrent requests, each holding one and waiting for a second, the pool deadlocks. Inside a loop it is worse. It can also deadlock on a row the outer transaction has locked. So I use it sparingly, never in a loop, and size the pool with it in mind."
Close "Join by default; start a new one only for work that must outlive the caller, and count the connections."

stages.name: Frame the axis
stages.html:
Propagation A transaction exists None exists
REQUIRED (default) join it start one
REQUIRES_NEW suspend it, start a new one start one
NESTED savepoint inside it start one
SUPPORTS join run without
MANDATORY join throw
NOT_SUPPORTED suspend, run without run without
NEVER throw run without

stages.name: Where REQUIRED fits
stages.html:
Flow:outer beginsinner joins the same transactionboth succeedone commit
Scenario Outcome
inner throws, outer doesn't catch everything rolls back
inner throws a runtime exception, outer catches and continues the transaction is marked rollback-only: the outer commit fails with UnexpectedRollbackException
outer throws after inner returned everything rolls back, including the inner work

stages.name: Where REQUIRES_NEW fits
stages.html:
Good uses Why
audit or attempt logging must be recorded even if the business action fails
a sequence or idempotency record must be visible to others immediately
an independent retryable step its failure shouldn't doom the caller

It only takes effect when the call goes through the proxy: an internal call on this silently joins the outer transaction.

stages.name: The deciding question
stages.html:
If the inner work Use
is part of the same business fact REQUIRED
must persist even when the caller rolls back REQUIRES_NEW
may fail without failing the caller, on plain JDBC NESTED (savepoint)
must never run outside a transaction MANDATORY
is a slow remote call no transaction at all around it

stages.name: What I'd pick here
stages.html:
pool size 10, 10 concurrent requests                      (illustrative)
each holds 1 connection (outer) and asks for a 2nd (REQUIRES_NEW)
connections needed = 20  >  10   →  all ten wait for a connection that none can release: pool deadlock
Hazard Symptom Guard
two connections per thread connection-timeout errors under load pool ≥ concurrent callers × 2 for that path, or restructure
REQUIRES_NEW in a loop a connection taken and returned per iteration; pool starved batch outside the loop
lock on a row the outer transaction holds the inner transaction waits for ever on its own caller don't touch the same rows
inner commit visible, outer rolled back inconsistent data if the inner work wasn't truly independent reserve it for audit-like records

Alternative for audit: publish an event and write the audit after commit or rollback with a transactional event listener, which avoids nested connections.

followUps.question: What is NESTED, and why is it rare?
followUps.html:
A savepoint inside the same transaction and connection.

REQUIRES_NEW NESTED
Connections two one
Inner rollback independent transaction back to the savepoint
Survives outer rollback yes no
Support everywhere JDBC savepoints; not with a JPA transaction manager by default

followUps.question: "I caught the exception from the inner method, so the outer commit is fine."
followUps.html:
Not with REQUIRED: the shared transaction is already marked rollback-only.

inner throwsproxy marks rollback-onlyouter catchesouter returnscommit attemptedUnexpectedRollbackException

followUps.question: Pool of 10, 6 concurrent requests on a path with one REQUIRES_NEW. Safe?
followUps.html:
It won't deadlock, but two requests will wait.

6 outer connections held + 4 inner available = pool full      → 2 requests wait for an inner connection
deadlock needs every connection held by an outer transaction: 10 or more concurrent requests

followUps.question: Does the inner transaction see the outer's uncommitted changes?
followUps.html:
No. It is a separate transaction on a separate connection.

  • Isolation applies between them as between any two transactions.
  • Reading a row the outer just inserted returns nothing, or blocks, by isolation level.

followUps.question: How would you detect misuse across a codebase?
followUps.html:
Search and measure.

  • Find every REQUIRES_NEW and ask "what must survive, and why?"
  • Pool metrics: active against max, wait time, timeouts.
  • A load test on those paths with concurrency above half the pool size.

dontSay: "REQUIRES_NEW is safer because it's isolated."
"Catching the exception saves the outer transaction."
"Propagation works on any method call" — only through the proxy.

java-spring-q18.testing: whether you can state what each actually buys (cheap blocking against backpressure and streaming), and what neither helps with.
java-spring-q18.trap: presenting virtual threads as free throughput, or reactive as generally faster.
java-spring-q18.spoken:
Beat Say
1 · Frame the axis "Both exist to serve many concurrent I/O-bound requests without one operating-system thread each. Virtual threads keep blocking code and make blocking cheap. Reactive replaces blocking with asynchronous pipelines."
2 · Where virtual threads win "With virtual threads I keep the imperative style: ordinary method calls, readable stack traces, the debugger, try-catch. A blocking call parks the virtual thread and frees the carrier. Ten thousand blocked tasks finish in about the time of one."
3 · Where reactive wins "Reactive gives backpressure as a first-class concept, which matters for streaming: a consumer can tell the producer to slow down. It also gives rich operators for composing asynchronous streams."
4 · The deciding question "So I ask: do I need streaming with backpressure, or just many concurrent blocking calls? And I remember what neither does: CPU-bound work gains nothing, and the database pool still caps me."
5 · What I'd pick here "In 2026 my default for a typical service is virtual threads on Spring MVC: simpler code, same scalability for request-response. I'd choose WebFlux where the workload is truly streaming, or where the team and the stack are already reactive."
Close "Virtual threads for most services, reactive for backpressure and streams, and neither for CPU-bound work."

stages.name: Frame the axis
stages.html:
Platform threads Virtual threads Reactive (WebFlux)
Cost per waiting request an OS thread, about a megabyte of stack a small heap object a callback
Code style blocking, imperative blocking, imperative asynchronous pipelines
Stack traces, debugger normal normal fragmented
Backpressure by pool and queue limits by semaphores and limits you add built in
Pick when few concurrent requests many concurrent blocking calls streaming, backpressure

stages.name: Where virtual threads win
stages.html:
Prove it — 10,000 tasks that each block for 200 ms (JDK 25):

import java.util.concurrent.*;
import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicInteger;
class Demo {
    public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception {
        AtomicInteger done = new AtomicInteger();
        long t0 = System.nanoTime();
        try (ExecutorService vt = Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor()) {
            for (int i = 0; i < 10_000; i++)
                vt.submit(() -> { Thread.sleep(200); return done.incrementAndGet(); });    // blocking call
        }                                                      // close() waits for all tasks
        long ms = (System.nanoTime() - t0) / 1_000_000;
        System.out.println("tasks finished: " + done.get());
        System.out.println("10,000 blocking tasks in under 3 s: " + (ms < 3000));
    }
}
// → tasks finished: 10000
// → 10,000 blocking tasks in under 3 s: true
What happens on a blocking call:virtual thread blocksit is unmounted from its carrierthe carrier runs another virtual threadwhen I/O completes, it is remounted
spring.threads.virtual.enabled=true        # Spring Boot 3.2+, on JDK 21+
Kept Why it matters
one request, one thread, one stack exceptions and profilers show the real call path
existing blocking libraries (JDBC, HTTP clients) no rewrite
thread-per-request mental model onboarding and debugging stay simple

stages.name: Where reactive wins
stages.html:
Capability Example
backpressure a slow WebSocket client makes the server produce less, instead of buffering without limit
stream composition merge, window, retry-with-backoff, timeout as operators
long-lived streaming endpoints server-sent events, token streams, change feeds
an end-to-end non-blocking stack reactive drivers (R2DBC), reactive HTTP client
Cost Detail
a different programming model everything returns Mono or Flux
one blocking call ruins it it stalls an event-loop thread shared by many requests
harder debugging stack traces show operators, not business flow
context thread-locals don't work: use the reactor context

stages.name: The deciding question
stages.html:
Workload Answer
request-response with blocking I/O, high concurrency virtual threads
streaming with consumers of varying speed reactive
CPU-bound computation neither: a bounded pool sized to the cores
limited by the database neither: the connection pool is the cap
Virtual-thread caveat Detail
pinning in synchronized JDK 21–23: a blocking call inside it holds the carrier; fixed in JDK 24
thread-locals a million virtual threads means a million copies: prefer scoped values or parameters
pooling virtual threads don't: create one per task; limit concurrency with a semaphore
downstream limits cheap threads make it easy to flood a database or an API

stages.name: What I'd pick here
stages.html:
Situation Choice
new CRUD or orchestration service Spring MVC + virtual threads
existing MVC service hitting thread-pool limits turn on virtual threads; test for pinning and pool limits
LLM token streaming, SSE fan-out, event gateways WebFlux, or MVC streaming with virtual threads if backpressure needs are modest
existing reactive service that works leave it

Evaluation hook: load-test both at the target concurrency and compare p99 latency, memory and error rate; the decision is then a measurement.

followUps.question: What is a carrier thread?
followUps.html:
A platform thread from a small pool that runs virtual threads.

Count
carriers about the number of cores
virtual threads as many as there are tasks

followUps.question: "Virtual threads make the service faster."
followUps.html:
They raise how many requests can wait at once; a single request isn't quicker.

Improves Doesn't improve
concurrency under blocking I/O latency of one call; CPU-bound throughput

followUps.question: After switching, the database starts timing out.
followUps.html:
The old thread pool was an accidental limiter, and it is gone.

Before:200 request threadsat most 200 concurrent queries
After:thousands of virtual threadsall wait on a pool of 20

Add an explicit concurrency limit (a semaphore or bulkhead) in front of the scarce resource.

followUps.question: How do you add backpressure with virtual threads?
followUps.html:
With ordinary blocking tools.

  • A Semaphore around a downstream call.
  • A bounded BlockingQueue between producer and consumer: put blocks when it is full.
  • Rate limiters and bulkheads from a resilience library.

followUps.question: Would you migrate a reactive codebase back?
followUps.html:
Only where the reactive style is costing more than it gives.

Keep reactive Consider migrating
streaming and backpressure are core plain request-response wrapped in Mono everywhere, with blocking calls offloaded

A migration is a rewrite of control flow; I'd do it service by service, starting where incidents come from.

dontSay: "Reactive is faster."
"Virtual threads are free performance."
"Pool your virtual threads."

java-spring-q19.testing: whether you know that constructor injection fails fast while field injection hides the cycle, and that the real fix is a design change.
java-spring-q19.spoken:
Beat Say
1 · Name it "A circular dependency: A needs B to be built, and B needs A. It is a design problem that shows up as a wiring problem."
2 · How Spring reacts "With constructor injection Spring can't build either, so startup fails with a bean-currently-in-creation error. With field or setter injection Spring can resolve it: it creates A, exposes an early reference, creates B with that reference, then finishes A. That 'works', which is the trap. Since Boot 2.6 circular references are refused by default either way."
3 · Confirm with evidence "The startup error prints the cycle as a small diagram of bean names, so I know exactly which edge to cut."
4 · Fix by experiment "The real fix is to remove the cycle. Usually both classes need a third thing: I extract that shared logic into its own bean that both depend on. Or one side only needs to notify the other, so I publish an event instead of calling. At-Lazy and ObjectProvider can break the cycle at run time, but the design is still circular."
5 · Validate "I'd validate by keeping circular references disallowed and letting the context start."
6 · Productionise "And I'd keep constructor injection everywhere, plus an architecture test that forbids package cycles."
Close "Constructor injection makes the cycle fail loudly; the fix is to extract or invert, not to defer."

stages.name: Name it
stages.claim: a design problem surfacing as wiring

stages.name: How Spring reacts
stages.html:
Injection Circular references disallowed (Boot 2.6+ default) Allowed (spring.main.allow-circular-references=true)
constructor startup fails startup fails: it can't be resolved at all
field or setter, singletons startup fails resolved through early references
prototype beans fails fails
How the early reference works:create A (raw)expose A through the early-reference cachecreate B, inject early Afinish Binject B into Afinish A

That mechanism is why field-injected cycles used to start silently, and why B may hold a reference to an A that wasn't fully initialised at that moment.

stages.name: Confirm with evidence
stages.html:
The dependencies of some of the beans in the application context form a cycle:
┌─────┐
|  orderService defined in file [...]
↑     ↓
|  paymentService defined in file [...]
└─────┘
Observation Likely cause Next action
BeanCurrentlyInCreationException with a cycle diagram a constructor cycle find the method each side calls on the other
app starts only with circular references allowed a field-injected cycle switch to constructors to see it
a NullPointerException in @PostConstruct an early reference used before it was ready remove the cycle
the cycle passes through three or more beans layering has eroded look at package dependencies, not just classes

stages.name: Fix by experiment
stages.html:
Experiment 1

Extract the shared concern

I'd move the logic both classes need into a third bean that depends on neither.

Why? Most cycles exist because two services each own half of one responsibility.

Best suited when each side calls one or two methods on the other.

Experiment 2

Invert with an event

I'd have A publish an event that B listens to, instead of A calling B.

Why? A no longer knows B exists; the dependency points one way.

Best suited when one direction is a notification, not a query.

Experiment 3

Defer the reference

I'd inject ObjectProvider<B> or mark one constructor parameter @Lazy.

Why? It breaks the cycle at construction time by injecting a proxy or a handle.

Best suited as a stopgap only: the classes are still mutually dependent.

stages.name: Validate
stages.claim: the context starts with cycles forbidden
stages.html:
Check Passes when
allow-circular-references left at false the application context starts
a context-load test in CI every profile wires without a cycle
unit tests of each class each can be constructed with fakes, in isolation

stages.name: Productionise
stages.html:
Guard Effect
constructor injection everywhere a new cycle fails at startup, in the pull request
an architecture test (for example ArchUnit: no package cycles) catches it before wiring does
layering rule dependencies point inward: web → service → domain
never enable circular references to "fix" a build it converts a loud failure into a quiet one

followUps.question: What does @Lazy actually inject?
followUps.html:
A proxy that resolves the real bean on first use.

construction: A gets a lazy proxy for BB is built normally with Afirst call on the proxylooks up the real B

followUps.question: "I added @Lazy and it starts, so it's fixed."
followUps.html:
The wiring starts; the design is unchanged.

Still true Consequence
A and B can't be understood or tested apart every change touches both
the first real call can still recurse a stack overflow at run time instead of a startup error

followUps.question: The cycle is between a bean and itself.
followUps.html:
That is self-injection, usually to reach the bean's own proxy.

  • Intent: call a @Transactional or @Cacheable method through advice.
  • Better: move that method to another bean.

followUps.question: Why did Boot change the default in 2.6?
followUps.html:
To make a design smell fail early instead of working by accident.

Before 2.6 From 2.6
field-injected cycles resolved silently refused unless explicitly allowed

followUps.question: A legacy codebase has forty cycles. Plan?
followUps.html:
Allow them temporarily, then burn the list down with a ratchet.

Plan:enable the flaglist every cyclefix by module, extracting shared piecesa test that fails if the count risesremove the flag

dontSay: "Use @Lazy."
"Switch to field injection, then it works."
"Set allow-circular-references to true."

java-spring-q20.testing: whether you know parallel streams run on one shared pool for the whole JVM, and can list the conditions under which they help.
java-spring-q20.trap: .parallel() on a stream that makes HTTP or database calls.
java-spring-q20.spoken:
Beat Say
1 · Frame the axis "A parallel stream splits the source, runs the pieces on the common ForkJoinPool, and merges the results. It trades coordination overhead for use of several cores."
2 · Where parallel wins "It helps when four things hold: a lot of data, a source that splits cheaply such as an array or ArrayList, work per element that is CPU-bound and non-trivial, and no shared mutable state."
3 · Where it is wrong "It is wrong when any of those fails. Small collections: overhead dominates. LinkedList or an iterator source: splitting is poor. Stateful lambdas: data races. And worst, blocking I/O: the common pool has about cores minus one threads for the entire JVM, so a few blocked tasks starve every other parallel stream and default CompletableFuture in the process."
4 · The deciding question "So I ask: is this CPU-bound, large, splittable and independent? And have I measured it?"
5 · What I'd pick here "In a request-handling service I rarely use it: requests already run in parallel across cores. For concurrent I/O I use an explicit executor or virtual threads. For batch computation it can be right, after a benchmark."
Close "Parallel streams are for big, splittable, CPU-bound, independent work; never for I/O on the shared pool."

stages.name: Frame the axis
stages.claim: split, compute, merge on a shared pool
stages.html:
How it runs:sourcespliterator splitstasks on the common ForkJoinPoolresults merged
Fact Consequence
one common pool per JVM parallel streams, default CompletableFuture tasks and others share it
parallelism ≈ available processors − 1 a handful of threads, plus the calling thread
the caller's thread also works a slow parallel stream holds the request thread too

stages.name: Where parallel wins
stages.html:
Condition Good Bad
size very many elements tens or hundreds
source splits cheaply array, ArrayList, IntStream.range LinkedList, Stream.iterate, I/O-backed iterators
work per element CPU-bound, non-trivial a field read, or anything that blocks
independence pure functions writes to shared state

Rule of thumb: elements × cost per element must be large enough to outweigh splitting and merging. That is a measurement, not a guess.

stages.name: Where it is wrong
stages.html:
Trace — a parallel stream that calls a slow HTTP endpoint (illustrative: 8 cores, so about 7 pool threads):

Time Common pool Everyone else in the JVM
request 1 starts .parallel() over 100 URLs all 7 workers blocked on HTTP —
request 2 uses a parallel stream for something cheap no free workers: runs mostly on its own thread slower
a default supplyAsync elsewhere queued behind blocked workers stalls
Failure Symptom
blocking I/O in the common pool unrelated features slow down together
shared mutable state (list.add inside forEach) missing elements, ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException, wrong totals
small N or cheap work slower than sequential
boxing (Stream<Integer> instead of IntStream) allocation overwhelms any gain
ordering-sensitive operations (limit, findFirst, forEachOrdered) expensive coordination, little speed-up

stages.name: The deciding question
stages.html:
Workload Use
CPU-heavy transform over a large array parallel stream, after a JMH benchmark
many blocking calls an explicit executor with CompletableFuture, or virtual threads
per-request work in a web service sequential: other requests already use the other cores
a pipeline with side effects sequential, or redesign to collect results

stages.name: What I'd pick here
stages.html:
long total = orders.parallelStream()                  // only if orders is large and price() is CPU work
    .mapToLong(Order::price)                          // primitive stream: no boxing
    .sum();                                           // an associative reduction, no shared state
Practice Why
collect, don't mutate: collect(toList()), never forEach(list::add) collectors are designed for parallel merging
primitive streams for numbers avoids boxing
benchmark with JMH intuition about parallel speed-ups is unreliable
never I/O the pool is shared

Thread-safety: lambdas in a parallel stream run on several threads at once. Anything they touch must be thread-safe or, better, untouched.

followUps.question: Can I run a parallel stream in my own pool?
followUps.html:
Submitting it from inside a custom ForkJoinPool works in practice, but it is an implementation detail.

Option Verdict
customPool.submit(() -> stream.parallel()…) works, undocumented behaviour
an executor with CompletableFuture the supported way to control threads

followUps.question: "Parallel is faster, we have 16 cores."
followUps.html:
Only if the cores are idle and the work fits the four conditions.

  • In a busy service the cores are already serving other requests.
  • For I/O cores aren't the limit at all.

followUps.question: Why is LinkedList bad here?
followUps.html:
It can't be split in the middle without walking it.

Source Split cost Balance
ArrayList, arrays O(1), by index even halves
LinkedList O(n) traversal uneven

followUps.question: Which operations need associativity?
followUps.html:
reduce and custom collectors.

(a op b) op c  must equal  a op (b op c)       ← sum, max, concat: yes;  subtraction, average-of-averages: no

followUps.question: How would you find a common-pool problem in production?
followUps.html:
A thread dump.

  • ForkJoinPool.commonPool-worker-* threads all blocked in socket reads or JDBC.
  • Request threads waiting in ForkJoinTask.join.
  • Fix: move the I/O to a dedicated executor; ban .parallel() on I/O in review.

dontSay: "Add .parallel() to speed it up."
"It uses all cores, so it's faster."
"forEach with list.add is fine."

java-spring-q21.testing: whether you can write it cleanly, and whether you volunteer the trade-off: one version is stateless and parallel-safe, the other is a stateful lambda.
java-spring-q21.trap: presenting the seen.add version without saying it breaks under .parallel().
java-spring-q21.spoken:
Beat Say
1 · Frame the axis "There are two idiomatic ways, and they differ in whether the lambda keeps state."
2 · The grouping solution "The clean one: group by the value itself and count, then keep the entries whose count is above one and take their keys. It is declarative, has no side effects, and works in parallel."
3 · The seen-set solution "The short one: keep a HashSet outside the stream and filter with 'not seen dot add of n'. Add returns false the second time, so only repeats pass. It is one pass and allocates less, but the lambda mutates shared state, so it is wrong in a parallel stream, and it emits a value once per extra occurrence unless I add distinct."
4 · The deciding question "So I ask: do I also need the counts, might this run in parallel, and does order matter?"
5 · What I'd pick here "I'd write the grouping version by default, with a LinkedHashMap if first-seen order matters, and mention that both depend on correct equals and hashCode for non-integer elements."
Close "Group and count for clarity and safety; the seen-set trick only for sequential streams."

stages.name: Frame the axis
stages.html:
Group and count Seen-set filter
Lambda state none mutates an external Set
Parallel-safe yes no
Gives counts too yes no
Passes over data one, plus one over the groups one
Extra memory a map of all distinct values a set of all distinct values
Pick when default; counts or parallel needed a quick sequential one-liner

stages.name: The grouping solution
stages.html:
Prove it — JDK 25:

import java.util.*;
import java.util.function.Function;
import java.util.stream.Collectors;
class Demo {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        List<Integer> nums = List.of(4, 7, 4, 9, 7, 4, 1);
        Set<Integer> dupes = nums.stream()
            .collect(Collectors.groupingBy(Function.identity(), LinkedHashMap::new, Collectors.counting()))
            .entrySet().stream()
            .filter(e -> e.getValue() > 1)
            .map(Map.Entry::getKey)
            .collect(Collectors.toCollection(LinkedHashSet::new));
        System.out.println(dupes);
        Set<Integer> seen = new HashSet<>();                    // one pass, but stateful: not for parallel streams
        System.out.println(nums.stream().filter(n -> !seen.add(n)).distinct().toList());
    }
}
// → [4, 7]
// → [4, 7]

Trace of [4, 7, 4, 9, 7, 4, 1] through the grouping version:

Step Result
groupingBy(identity(), LinkedHashMap::new, counting()) {4=3, 7=2, 9=1, 1=1}
filter(count > 1) {4=3, 7=2}
map(getKey) [4, 7]

LinkedHashMap::new keeps first-seen order. The default groupingBy returns a HashMap, whose order is unspecified.

stages.name: The seen-set solution
stages.html:
How it works:seen.add(n) returns true the first time!true filters it outlater occurrences return falsethey pass
Caveat Detail
stateful lambda the stream documentation warns against it; in a parallel stream HashSet is corrupted or results vary
repeats of repeats 4 appears three times, so it passes twice: add .distinct() or collect to a set

stages.name: The deciding question
stages.html:
Requirement Choice
just the duplicate values, sequential either
need how many times each occurs grouping
may run in parallel grouping (groupingByConcurrent for very large inputs)
first-seen order grouping into a LinkedHashMap
sorted output grouping into a TreeMap, or sort the keys
very large input, memory-sensitive sort then compare neighbours, or use a primitive-specialised structure

stages.name: What I'd pick here
stages.claim: and what I'd say while writing it
stages.html:
Point to say aloud Why it scores
"Function.identity() groups by the element itself" shows fluency
"counting() returns Long" so the filter compares with 1, a long
"order needs a LinkedHashMap supplier" anticipates the follow-up
"for custom objects this relies on equals and hashCode" ties to the map-key contract
"without streams: a HashSet and a loop is just as good" streams aren't mandatory

Complexity: O(n) time and O(distinct) space for both.

followUps.question: Do it with Collections.frequency.
followUps.html:
It works and is quadratic.

nums.stream().filter(n -> Collections.frequency(nums, n) > 1).collect(Collectors.toSet());   // O(n²)

Fine for a handful of elements, wrong for a large list.

followUps.question: "The seen.add filter is the best answer: one line, one pass."
followUps.html:
It is the shortest, and it has a side effect inside a stream operation.

Run as Result
sequential correct
parallel data race on the HashSet: wrong or inconsistent output

followUps.question: The list has 50 million integers.
followUps.html:
Avoid boxing and a giant map of Integer to Long.

  • Use int[] and sort: equal neighbours are the duplicates.
  • Or a bit set if the value range is bounded.
  • Streams of boxed Integer would allocate heavily here.

followUps.question: Find the first duplicate instead.
followUps.html:
The seen-set approach, stopped at the first hit.

Set<Integer> seen = new HashSet<>();
Optional<Integer> first = nums.stream().filter(n -> !seen.add(n)).findFirst();     // sequential only

followUps.question: Would you use a stream for this in production code?
followUps.html:
Whichever reads most clearly to the team.

Version Reads as
grouping collector "count each, keep those above one"
plain loop with a set equally clear, slightly faster, no surprises

The interview asks for streams; code review asks for clarity.

dontSay: The seen.add trick with no caveat.
"groupingBy keeps the original order."
"distinct() gives the duplicates" — it removes them.

java-spring-q22.testing: whether you place a cross-cutting concern by the layer that has the information it needs.
java-spring-q22.trap: an aspect for authorisation that never fires on an internal call.
java-spring-q22.spoken:
Beat Say
1 · Frame the axis "All three wrap behaviour around a request or a call. They sit at different layers and so know different things."
2 · Where a filter fits "A filter is at the servlet level, before Spring MVC. It sees every request, including ones that match no controller, and it can wrap the request and response bodies. It knows nothing about which handler will run. That suits security, CORS, compression and request IDs."
3 · Where an interceptor fits "An interceptor is inside Spring MVC. It knows the handler method, so it can read its annotations, and it has pre-handle, post-handle and after-completion hooks. That suits handler-aware concerns: timing per endpoint, tenant resolution, locale."
4 · Where an aspect fits "An aspect wraps any bean method, not just web requests, with access to arguments and the return value. That suits service-layer concerns: transactions, caching, retries, auditing. But it is proxy-based, so calls through 'this' are not advised."
5 · The deciding question "So I ask what the concern needs to know: just HTTP, the handler, or the method arguments and result; and whether it must also apply to non-web callers."
Close "Protocol-level in a filter, handler-aware in an interceptor, method-level in an aspect."

stages.name: Frame the axis
stages.html:
Order on a request:filtersDispatcherServletinterceptorscontrolleraspects around service beansrepository
Filter Interceptor Aspect
Layer servlet container Spring MVC any Spring bean
Sees unmatched URLs, static resources yes no no
Knows the handler method no yes n/a
Can wrap or replace request and response bodies yes no no
Sees method arguments and return value no no yes
Applies to non-web callers (schedulers, listeners) no no yes
Limitation no MVC context can't change the body stream proxy-bound

stages.name: Where a filter fits
stages.html:
Concern Why a filter
authentication must run before anything else; Spring Security is a filter chain
CORS, compression, character encoding pure HTTP
request ID and MDC setup should cover every request, including 404s
request and response body logging needs to wrap the streams, which are read once
rate limiting at the edge reject before MVC does any work

Exceptions thrown here are not handled by @ControllerAdvice.

stages.name: Where an interceptor fits
stages.html:
Hook Runs Use
preHandle before the controller; can stop the request check an annotation on the handler; resolve tenant
postHandle after the controller, before the view or body is finalised add model attributes
afterCompletion always, after the response timing, cleanup

Trace — timing per endpoint:

Step Action
preHandle store start time in a request attribute
controller runs
afterCompletion compute elapsed, tag the metric with the handler method name

A filter couldn't tag by handler; it doesn't know which one ran.

stages.name: Where an aspect fits
stages.html:
@Aspect @Component
class AuditAspect {
    @Around("@annotation(Audited)")                       // any bean method carrying @Audited
    Object audit(ProceedingJoinPoint pjp) throws Throwable {
        Object result = pjp.proceed();                    // arguments and result are both available
        return result;
    }
}
Concern Why an aspect
transactions, caching, retries they wrap a method's execution and outcome
auditing with business arguments needs the parameters and return value
applies to scheduled jobs and message listeners too not tied to HTTP
Limitation Consequence
proxy-based self-invocation, private and final methods are not advised
indirection behaviour that isn't visible at the call site

stages.name: The deciding question
stages.claim: what does the concern need to know
stages.html:
The concern needs Use
only the HTTP request or response, for every request filter
to change the body filter
the handler method or its annotations interceptor
method arguments, return value, or exceptions of a service aspect
to apply outside web requests aspect
authorisation that must not be bypassed filter-chain URL rules plus method security on service entry points

Why this matters: each extra layer adds stack depth and a place to look during debugging, so one concern goes in one layer.

followUps.question: In what order do they run?
followUps.html:
Outside in on the request, inside out on the response.

filter ininterceptor preHandleaspect beforemethodaspect afterinterceptor postHandlefilter out

followUps.question: "Put authorisation in an aspect, it's the most flexible."
followUps.html:
Flexible, and bypassable from inside the class.

Call Aspect fires?
controller → service method yes
service method → another method on this no

Keep URL-level rules in the filter chain as the outer guard.

followUps.question: I need to log the request body and the handler name together.
followUps.html:
Two layers cooperating.

  • Filter: wraps the request in a caching wrapper so the body can be read again.
  • Interceptor afterCompletion: reads the cached body and the handler, and logs both.

followUps.question: How do you order several filters or aspects?
followUps.html:
Explicitly.

Kind Ordering
filters @Order or a FilterRegistrationBean order
interceptors registration order in WebMvcConfigurer
aspects @Order: lower runs first on the way in

followUps.question: When do you avoid all three?
followUps.html:
When the behaviour is core logic, not cross-cutting.

Sign Do instead
the rule applies to two methods call a helper explicitly
reviewers can't tell what a method does without knowing the aspects make it visible in the code

dontSay: "They're interchangeable."
"Use an aspect for security."
"Interceptors can modify the request body."

java-spring-q23.testing: whether you connect the exception style to transaction rollback and to where errors are translated to HTTP.
java-spring-q23.trap: not mentioning that @Transactional rolls back on unchecked exceptions only, by default.
java-spring-q23.spoken:
Beat Say
1 · Frame the axis "A checked exception forces every caller to handle or declare it. An unchecked one doesn't. The question is whether the caller can do something useful about it."
2 · Where unchecked fits "In a service layer I lean unchecked. Most failures, such as not found, a rule violated, a conflict, can't be recovered by the immediate caller; they travel up to the edge. Checked exceptions there just leak through every signature, or get wrapped and swallowed."
3 · Where checked fits "Checked is defensible where the caller really can and must react: a retryable condition at an integration boundary, for example."
4 · The deciding question "So I ask: will the direct caller handle this differently from any other failure? If not, unchecked."
5 · What I'd pick here "My design: a small hierarchy of unchecked domain exceptions, thrown by services, mapped to HTTP problem responses in one controller advice. And the choice has a transactional consequence: Spring rolls back on unchecked exceptions and commits on checked ones by default. So a checked business exception inside a transaction leaves partial data unless I declare rollback-for."
Close "Unchecked domain exceptions, translated at the edge, with rollback behaviour understood."

stages.name: Frame the axis
stages.html:
Checked Unchecked
Compiler forces handling yes no
Appears in signatures yes: every layer up no
Works with lambdas and streams awkwardly yes
Spring default on @Transactional commit roll back
Pick when the direct caller can recover the failure is handled at the edge

stages.name: Where unchecked fits
stages.claim: failures that travel to the edge
stages.html:
The path of a domain failure:service throws OrderNotFoundExceptionpasses through callers untouched@RestControllerAdvice maps it404 with a problem body
Reason Detail
no signature pollution intermediate layers don't declare or wrap it
framework convention Spring's own data-access exceptions are unchecked for this reason
rollback by default a failed use case leaves no partial writes

stages.name: Where checked fits
stages.html:
Case Why checked can be right
an integration client whose caller must choose retry, fallback or abort the decision is local and mandatory
a library API with a recoverable, expected condition the compiler reminds the user
parsing user input where "invalid" is a normal outcome though a result type often reads better

Even then, a sealed result type (Success or Failure) is a modern alternative that makes the outcome explicit without exceptions.

stages.name: The deciding question
stages.html:
Thrown inside @Transactional Default To change it
RuntimeException or Error roll back noRollbackFor = …
checked exception commit rollbackFor = Exception.class
caught inside the method and not rethrown commit rethrow, or setRollbackOnly()

Example: transfer() debits account A, then throws a checked InsufficientFundsException while crediting B. With defaults the debit commits. Money has vanished, and no error says so.

stages.name: What I'd pick here
stages.claim: a hierarchy mapped at the edge
stages.html:
abstract class DomainException extends RuntimeException { /* code, message */ }
class NotFoundException extends DomainException { }
class ConflictException extends DomainException { }
class RuleViolationException extends DomainException { }

@RestControllerAdvice
class ApiErrors {
    @ExceptionHandler(NotFoundException.class)
    ProblemDetail notFound(NotFoundException e) { return ProblemDetail.forStatusAndDetail(HttpStatus.NOT_FOUND, e.getMessage()); }
}
Rule Why
services throw domain exceptions, never HTTP types the service is reusable from jobs and listeners
one advice class maps them to status codes consistent API errors
wrap low-level exceptions with the cause attached the stack trace keeps the root
never catch (Exception e) {} it hides failures and, in a transaction, commits them
never throws Exception on a public API it tells the caller nothing

followUps.question: Why does Spring commit on checked exceptions?
followUps.html:
It follows the EJB convention: checked means an expected business outcome, unchecked means a failure.

Convention Treats as
checked an alternative return value: commit
unchecked a system failure: roll back

Most teams don't use checked exceptions that way, hence the surprise.

followUps.question: "Checked exceptions are safer because the compiler enforces handling."
followUps.html:
It enforces a catch block, not a correct one.

  • Common result: catch (Exception e) { log.error(…); } and execution continues.
  • In a transaction that continues to a commit.

followUps.question: A lambda in a stream needs to call a method that throws a checked exception.
followUps.html:
Functional interfaces don't declare it, so it must be handled or wrapped inside the lambda.

Option Trade
wrap in an unchecked exception simple; keep the cause
return a result type per element failures become data
use a loop often the clearest

followUps.question: Where do validation errors go?
followUps.html:
Input validation at the web edge, business rules in the domain.

Kind Raised by Status
malformed input bean validation on the request 400
business rule a domain exception 409 or 422

followUps.question: How do you keep error handling consistent across forty services?
followUps.html:
Share the contract, not the stack traces.

  • A common problem-details format (RFC 9457) with stable error codes.
  • A shared starter with the base exception types and the advice.
  • Contract tests that assert status and error code for the main failures.

dontSay: "Checked exceptions are always better / always bad."
"Any exception rolls back the transaction."
"Catch Exception and log it."
