java-spring-q24.testing: whether you can argue from object validity, testability and visibility of design problems, not from habit.
java-spring-q24.spoken:
Beat Say
1 · Frame the axis "The question is when and how an object receives its collaborators: at construction, visibly, or afterwards, by reflection."
2 · Where constructor wins "With constructor injection the dependencies are explicit in the signature, the fields can be final, and the object can't exist in a half-built state. A unit test is just 'new' with fakes; no container, no reflection."
3 · Where field falls short "Field injection hides the dependencies inside the class, needs reflection or a Spring context to test, allows null fields if someone constructs it directly, and hides circular dependencies that a constructor would expose at startup."
4 · The deciding question "So I ask: could I construct and test this class without Spring? With constructor injection the answer is always yes."
5 · What I'd pick here "Constructor injection for everything required. Setter injection only for a truly optional collaborator. And when a constructor grows to eight parameters, that isn't a DI problem: the class is telling me it does too much. Boilerplate isn't an argument either: a single constructor needs no annotation, and a record or Lombok writes it."
Close "Constructor injection: explicit, final, always valid, testable with plain new."

stages.name: Frame the axis
stages.claim: visible at construction, or injected later
stages.html:
Constructor Setter Field
Dependencies visible in the API yes partly no
final fields yes no no
Object valid after new yes not until setters run no: fields are null
Test without Spring new X(fake) call setters reflection or a context
Cycle fails at startup yes resolved silently (if allowed) resolved silently (if allowed)
Pick when required dependencies optional ones legacy code and tests only

stages.name: Where constructor wins
stages.html:
Prove it — the class and its test need no container (JDK 25):

class Demo {
    interface PaymentGateway { boolean charge(int cents); }
    static class OrderService {
        private final PaymentGateway gateway;                  // final: set once, never null
        OrderService(PaymentGateway gateway) { this.gateway = java.util.Objects.requireNonNull(gateway); }
        String place(int cents) { return gateway.charge(cents) ? "PLACED" : "DECLINED"; }
    }
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        OrderService ok = new OrderService(cents -> true);     // a test: no container, no reflection
        OrderService declined = new OrderService(cents -> false);
        System.out.println(ok.place(500) + " " + declined.place(500));
        try { new OrderService(null); }
        catch (NullPointerException e) { System.out.println("missing dependency fails at construction"); }
    }
}
// → PLACED DECLINED
// → missing dependency fails at construction
Property shown Benefit
fake supplied through the constructor fast, isolated unit tests
final field safe publication; no reassignment
null rejected at construction failure at wiring time, not at first use

In Spring, a class with one constructor needs no @Autowired (since 4.3).

stages.name: Where field falls short
stages.html:
@Service
class OrderService {
    @Autowired private PaymentGateway gateway;        // invisible to callers; null after `new OrderService()`
}
Cost Consequence
hidden dependencies the class's needs aren't in its API
reflection to set them tests need @SpringBootTest, @InjectMocks or ReflectionTestUtils
mutable, non-final fields weaker thread-safety guarantees
cycles hidden a design problem that constructor injection would report at startup
easy to add "just one more" classes grow to fifteen dependencies unnoticed

stages.name: The deciding question
stages.claim: does it work without the container
stages.html:
Situation Choice
a required collaborator constructor
an optional collaborator with a sensible default setter, or ObjectProvider<T> / Optional<T> in the constructor
test classes field injection is acceptable: nobody constructs a test by hand
framework-managed types that need a no-arg constructor (JPA entities) they shouldn't have injected services at all

stages.name: What I'd pick here
stages.html:
@Service
class OrderService {
    private final PaymentGateway gateway;
    private final OrderRepository orders;
    OrderService(PaymentGateway gateway, OrderRepository orders) { this.gateway = gateway; this.orders = orders; }
}
A constructor with many parameters means Response
the class has several responsibilities split it by use case
several parameters always travel together group them into one collaborator
a facade is forming name it and give it a narrower API

Thread-safety: final fields set in the constructor are safely published to every thread that later uses the singleton.

followUps.question: Why does final matter beyond style?
followUps.html:
The memory model guarantees final fields are visible, fully initialised, to all threads after construction.

Field Visibility to other threads
final, set in the constructor guaranteed
non-final, set later by reflection relies on the container's own synchronisation

followUps.question: "Field injection is less boilerplate."
followUps.html:
The boilerplate is one constructor, which tools write.

  • Lombok @RequiredArgsConstructor, or a record-style component.
  • No @Autowired needed on a single constructor.
  • What field injection saves in typing it costs in testing.

followUps.question: Constructor injection made my circular dependency fail at startup.
followUps.html:
That is the feature: the cycle existed before, it was just hidden.

constructor cyclestartup errorextract the shared piece or invert with an event

followUps.question: How do I inject configuration values?
followUps.html:
Also through the constructor, ideally as a typed properties object.

@ConfigurationProperties("payments")
record PaymentProps(Duration timeout, int maxRetries) { }        // bound and validated at startup

followUps.question: A codebase has a thousand @Autowired fields. Worth migrating?
followUps.html:
Incrementally, where it pays.

Do Skip
new code, and classes being changed anyway a big-bang rewrite
classes with slow context-based tests stable leaf classes nobody touches

An IDE inspection or an automated refactoring recipe does most of the mechanical work.

dontSay: "Field injection, it's cleaner."
"Constructor injection causes circular dependency errors" — it reveals them.
"The constructor has too many arguments, so use fields."

java-spring-q25.testing: whether you see records as immutable data carriers with value semantics, and know the place they don't fit.
java-spring-q25.spoken:
Beat Say
1 · Plain definition "A record is a transparent, shallowly immutable carrier for a fixed set of values. I declare the components, and the class is its data."
2 · What the compiler generates "The compiler generates private final fields, a canonical constructor, an accessor per component, and equals, hashCode and toString based on all components. A compact constructor lets me validate and normalise before the fields are assigned."
3 · Where they break "They don't fit where a framework needs mutability and a no-argument constructor, which means JPA entities. They can't extend a class. And the immutability is shallow: a record holding a mutable list can still be changed through that list."
4 · Where I use them "I use them for DTOs at API boundaries, value objects such as Money, events, configuration properties, query projections, and map keys, since immutability with value equality is exactly what a key needs."
5 · Adjacent concept "Paired with sealed interfaces they give algebraic data types: a closed set of record variants and a switch the compiler checks for exhaustiveness."
Close "Records for data that is what it holds; classes for things with identity and lifecycle."

stages.name: Plain definition
stages.html:
Record Ordinary class JPA entity
Fields final, one per component anything mutable
Equality by value, all components identity unless overridden by identifier, carefully
Inheritance implicitly final; may implement interfaces free free
Purpose carry data behaviour and state persistent identity

stages.name: What the compiler generates
stages.html:
Prove it — JDK 25:

import java.util.*;
class Demo {
    record Money(long cents, String currency) {
        Money {                                                // compact constructor: validate and normalise
            if (cents < 0) throw new IllegalArgumentException("negative amount");
            currency = currency.toUpperCase();
        }
    }
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        Money a = new Money(500, "inr"), b = new Money(500, "INR");
        System.out.println(a + " equals b: " + a.equals(b));
        Map<Money, String> prices = new HashMap<>(Map.of(a, "coffee"));
        System.out.println(prices.get(b));                     // safe as a map key: immutable, value equality
        try { new Money(-1, "INR"); } catch (IllegalArgumentException e) { System.out.println(e.getMessage()); }
    }
}
// → Money[cents=500, currency=INR] equals b: true
// → coffee
// → negative amount
Generated From record Money(long cents, String currency)
fields private final long cents; private final String currency;
canonical constructor assigns both; the compact form runs my checks first
accessors cents(), currency(): no get prefix
equals, hashCode from all components
toString Money[cents=500, currency=INR]

The snippet shows normalisation making "inr" and "INR" equal, the record working as a map key, and validation rejecting a negative amount.

stages.name: Where they break
stages.html:
Limit Detail Consequence
not for JPA entities entities need a no-arg constructor, non-final fields for proxies and dirty checking use records for projections and DTOs instead
no class inheritance a record extends java.lang.Record implicitly model variants with a sealed interface
shallow immutability a List component can be mutated by whoever holds it copy in the compact constructor: items = List.copyOf(items)
all components are public API accessors are generated for each don't put secrets or internal state in one
arrays as components equals compares references use a list

stages.name: Where I use them
stages.html:
Use Example
request and response DTOs record CreateOrder(String sku, int qty) with validation annotations on components
value objects Money, EmailAddress, DateRange with invariants in the compact constructor
events and messages record OrderPlaced(UUID id, Instant at)
configuration @ConfigurationProperties records, bound through the constructor
query projections Spring Data interface or constructor projections into a record
map keys and set elements immutable, value-based hashCode
several return values a small local record instead of an array or a Map

Thread-safety: a record whose components are themselves immutable is safe to share freely.

stages.name: Adjacent concept
stages.html:
sealed interface PaymentResult permits Approved, Declined, Pending { }
record Approved(String authCode) implements PaymentResult { }
record Declined(String reason) implements PaymentResult { }
record Pending(Instant retryAt) implements PaymentResult { }

String describe(PaymentResult r) {
    return switch (r) {                                   // no default: the compiler checks every case
        case Approved a -> "ok " + a.authCode();
        case Declined d -> "no: " + d.reason();
        case Pending p -> "retry at " + p.retryAt();
    };
}

Add a fourth variant and every such switch stops compiling until it is handled. That is the benefit over an enum plus nullable fields.

followUps.question: Record or Lombok @Value?
followUps.html:
A record when the type is pure data; Lombok when you need what records forbid.

Record Lombok @Value
Language feature yes annotation processor
Can extend a class no yes
Pattern matching and deconstruction yes no

followUps.question: "Make the JPA entities records to cut boilerplate."
followUps.html:
Entities need what records forbid.

JPA needs Record gives
no-arg constructor, mutable fields, subclassable for lazy proxies final class, final fields, canonical constructor only

Use records for the DTOs and projections around the entities.

followUps.question: Is a record with a List component immutable?
followUps.html:
Only if the constructor makes a defensive copy.

record Order(List<String> items) { Order { items = List.copyOf(items); } }     // unmodifiable snapshot

followUps.question: Can a record have methods and static members?
followUps.html:
Yes: instance methods, static methods and static fields. No extra instance fields.

  • Derived values as methods: boolean isZero().
  • Factories as static methods: Money.ofRupees(5).

followUps.question: Any serialisation concerns?
followUps.html:
Mostly benefits, and one compatibility point.

Aspect Note
Jackson binds through the canonical constructor; component names are the JSON fields
API evolution adding a component changes the constructor: treat a public DTO record as a contract
Java serialisation records are deserialised through the constructor, so invariants hold

dontSay: "Records replace classes."
"Use records for entities."
"Records are deeply immutable."

java-spring-q26.testing: whether you know the real technical difference (run-time against build-time wiring) and are honest that people and ecosystem usually decide.
java-spring-q26.spoken:
Beat Say
1 · Frame the axis "The technical axis is when dependency injection and configuration are resolved. Spring traditionally does it at run time, with reflection and classpath scanning at startup. Micronaut and Quarkus do most of it at build time."
2 · Where Spring wins "Spring has the largest ecosystem, the most integrations, the most documentation and the biggest hiring pool. For a long-running service, startup time is paid once and doesn't matter."
3 · Where the others win "Build-time wiring gives fast startup and a small memory footprint, and fits native images well. That matters for serverless functions, scale-to-zero workloads, and very dense deployments where each pod's memory is money."
4 · The deciding question "So I ask: is startup time or memory per instance a first-order constraint? And is the team already productive in Spring?"
5 · What I'd pick here "Usually Spring. Spring Boot 3's ahead-of-time processing and native-image support closed much of the gap, so the argument is weaker than it was a few years ago. I'd pick Quarkus or Micronaut for a function platform or a fleet of tiny services where cold start is the product, and only with a team willing to own it."
Close "Spring by default; a build-time framework when cold start or density is the requirement."

stages.name: Frame the axis
stages.html:
Run-time wiring (classic Spring):start JVMscan classpathread annotations by reflectionbuild bean graphcreate proxiesready
Build-time wiring (Micronaut, Quarkus, Spring AOT): compileannotation processing or build-time augmentation generates the wiring codestart JVMrun generated codeready
Spring Boot (JVM) Spring Boot (AOT + native) Micronaut Quarkus
DI resolved run time build time compile time build time
Reflection use heavy reduced, with hints minimal minimal
Startup, memory highest low low low
Ecosystem largest same, minus what isn't native-ready smaller smaller, strong for Kubernetes

stages.name: Where Spring wins
stages.html:
Strength Why it matters
integrations for almost everything data stores, messaging, security, cloud, AI
hiring pool and shared knowledge most Java engineers already know it
mature operations story actuator, observability, config, testing slices
long-running services startup cost is paid once per deploy
Spring AI and MCP support relevant when the service gains an LLM layer

stages.name: Where the others win
stages.html:
Workload Why build-time DI helps
serverless functions every cold start is user-visible latency
scale-to-zero services the first request pays the startup
hundreds of small pods memory per instance multiplies
CLI tools and short batch jobs startup is most of the run time
native images less reflection means fewer hints and surprises

Trade-offs of native images in any framework: long build times, no JIT warm-up gains at peak, and reflection-heavy libraries need configuration.

stages.name: The deciding question
stages.html:
Question If yes
is cold start or memory per instance a hard requirement? consider Quarkus, Micronaut, or Spring native
does a critical library lack support outside Spring? Spring
is the team fluent in Spring and nothing else? Spring, unless the constraint is severe
is it a long-running service behind a load balancer? Spring: the difference won't be felt
will the platform team support a second framework? if not, don't add one

stages.name: What I'd pick here
stages.html:
Situation Choice
typical business service Spring Boot on the JVM
Spring service that needs faster start Spring AOT, class-data sharing, then native image if required
function platform, cold start is the SLO Quarkus or Micronaut, or Spring native after measuring
greenfield in a Kubernetes-native shop already on Quarkus Quarkus

Evaluation hook: measure startup time, memory at steady state and p99 latency under load on your service skeleton, in both candidates, before deciding.

followUps.question: What does Spring AOT actually do?
followUps.html:
It moves bean-definition processing to build time and generates code for it.

Run time before With AOT
scan, parse configuration, evaluate conditions pre-computed bean definitions and reflection hints

It also fixes the set of beans at build time, so some run-time conditions no longer vary.

followUps.question: "Quarkus is ten times faster, so we should migrate."
followUps.html:
Faster to start. Steady-state request handling depends on your code and I/O.

Metric Affected by the framework choice
startup, idle memory strongly
p99 latency of a database-bound endpoint barely

A migration costs months; the benefit must be something users or the bill can see.

followUps.question: A JVM service is slow to start but must stay on Spring.
followUps.html:
There is a ladder before native.

lazy initialisation where safetrim auto-configurationclass-data sharing / AOT cacheSpring AOT on the JVMnative image

followUps.question: Is native always better for containers?
followUps.html:
No: it trades peak throughput and build time for startup and memory.

JVM Native image
Startup slower very fast
Peak throughput after warm-up higher (JIT) often lower
Build time short long

followUps.question: How do you make this decision stick in an organisation?
followUps.html:
Write the criteria down, with a default.

  • Default framework for services, with the platform team's support.
  • Named exceptions: workloads with a cold-start or footprint SLO.
  • A review when someone proposes a second framework: who maintains the templates, pipelines and on-call knowledge.

dontSay: "Spring is slow."
"Quarkus is faster" without saying at what.
"We should use the newest framework."

java-spring-q27.testing: whether you distinguish the per-session cache from the shared one, and treat invalidation across nodes as the real problem.
java-spring-q27.trap: enabling the second-level cache globally and creating stale reads across the cluster.
java-spring-q27.spoken:
Beat Say
1 · Frame the axis "There are three layers: the first-level cache inside each session, the optional second-level cache shared across sessions, and the query cache on top of that."
2 · The first-level cache "The first level is the persistence context. It is always on, lives for one session or transaction, and guarantees that loading the same entity twice returns the same object. It isn't a performance cache across requests."
3 · Where second-level fits "The second level stores entity data by ID outside the session, in a provider such as Ehcache, Infinispan or Redis. I opt in per entity. It pays for read-mostly reference data: countries, product categories, feature settings."
4 · Where it hurts "It hurts on entities that change often, and in a cluster. Every node needs to learn about every change, so I need a distributed or invalidating cache; otherwise nodes serve different answers. Anything that writes to the database outside Hibernate bypasses it entirely. And the query cache is the easiest to get wrong: any change to a table invalidates every cached query on it."
5 · What I'd enable "So: first level always, second level for a short list of read-mostly entities with an explicit concurrency strategy, and the query cache rarely. Before any of it I check that the real problem isn't N plus one."
Close "L1 always, L2 by entity for reference data, query cache last."

stages.name: Frame the axis
stages.html:
Layer Scope On by default Stores Keyed by
first level (persistence context) one session / transaction yes, can't be disabled managed entity instances entity type + ID
second level the whole application, across sessions no entity state (not objects) entity type + ID
query cache the whole application no lists of IDs for a query + parameters query string + parameters

stages.name: The first-level cache
stages.html:
Lookup order for find(Order, 42): first level ─hit─▶ return the managed instance

On a miss:second level (if enabled for the entity)databaseput in both
What it gives What it doesn't
repeatable reads within the session nothing across requests
one object per row: find twice returns the same instance protection from N+1: associations still load one by one
the base for dirty checking and write-behind bounded memory: a long session accumulates every entity it touches

Batch jobs: flush and clear the session periodically, or the first-level cache grows until memory runs out.

stages.name: Where second-level fits
stages.html:
@Entity
@Cache(usage = CacheConcurrencyStrategy.READ_ONLY)        // opt in, per entity, with a strategy
class Country { @Id String code; String name; }
Concurrency strategy Use for Cost
READ_ONLY data that never changes cheapest
NONSTRICT_READ_WRITE rare updates, brief staleness acceptable low
READ_WRITE updates with consistency through soft locks higher
TRANSACTIONAL full transactional caches (JTA) highest
Good candidate Bad candidate
small, read constantly, changed rarely large, updated often, or user-specific

stages.name: Where it hurts
stages.html:
Hazard Symptom Guard
several nodes, local caches node A shows the new value, node B the old a distributed or invalidation-replicated provider
writes outside Hibernate (SQL scripts, another service, bulk JPQL updates) cache never learns of them evict explicitly; or don't cache that entity
hot mutable entities constant invalidation, lock overhead, no hits don't cache them
query cache on a busy table every write to the table evicts all cached results for it reserve it for near-static tables
associations not cached the entity is cached, its collection still queries cache the collection separately, deliberately
memory heap pressure from a large region size limits and expiry per region

stages.name: What I'd enable
stages.html:
Step Action
0 fix N+1 and missing indexes first: caching a bad access pattern hides it
1 L1: nothing to do, but keep sessions short
2 L2 for a named list of reference entities, READ_ONLY or NONSTRICT_READ_WRITE, with size and expiry
3 a cluster-aware provider if there is more than one node
4 query cache only for queries over those same static entities
5 statistics on: hit ratio per region decides whether a region stays

Alternative: an explicit application cache (@Cacheable on a service method returning DTOs) is often simpler to reason about than L2, because the key and the invalidation are in my code.

Evaluation hook: hit ratio, eviction count and query count per request, before and after.

followUps.question: Why does the query cache need the second-level cache?
followUps.html:
It stores IDs, not entities.

cached query result = list of IDseach ID is looked up in L2without L2, each becomes a database query

So a query cache without L2 can turn one query into N.

followUps.question: "Turn on L2 for everything; fewer queries is always good."
followUps.html:
For changing data it means stale reads or constant invalidation.

Entity L2 effect
reference data high hit ratio, big win
orders, balances, anything hot low hit ratio, overhead, staleness risk

followUps.question: A nightly SQL script updates prices. Users see old prices next morning.
followUps.html:
The script bypassed Hibernate, so the cache was never invalidated.

  • Evict the region after the job (cache.evictRegion), or route the update through the application.
  • Or set an expiry short enough to bound the staleness.

followUps.question: Does getReference or a JPQL query use the first-level cache?
followUps.html:
Lookups by ID do; queries always go to the database.

Call Hits L1 before the database
find(id) yes
JPQL or criteria query no: it runs, then reuses managed instances for rows already in the context

followUps.question: L2 or an application-level cache?
followUps.html:
L2 for entity-by-ID lookups Hibernate does implicitly; an application cache for use-case results.

Second-level cache Application cache
Granularity entity state any computed result or DTO
Invalidation by Hibernate, if all writes go through it explicit, in your code
Visibility implicit visible at the call site

dontSay: "Hibernate caches everything automatically."
"Enable the second-level cache to fix slow queries."
"The first-level cache speeds up repeated requests."

java-spring-q28.testing: whether you can explain why it happens, pick a fix per use case, and name the pagination trap and a test that keeps it from returning.
java-spring-q28.spoken:
Beat Say
1 · Name it "N plus one is one query that loads N parent rows, followed by one more query per parent to load a lazy association. It is invisible with ten rows in development and catastrophic with ten thousand in production."
2 · Rule out the fakes "I'd first make sure it is that, and not a single slow query or a missing index: the signature is many small, near-identical statements."
3 · Confirm with evidence "I confirm by counting statements for one request, with SQL logging or Hibernate statistics. Five orders producing six queries is the pattern."
4 · Fix by experiment "The fix depends on the use case. For one screen that needs parents with children: a JOIN FETCH query or an entity graph, so it is one statement. For large or several collections: batch fetching, which loads children for many parents with an IN clause. And when I only need a few columns, a DTO projection, with no entities at all."
5 · Validate "Then I assert the query count in a test for that use case."
6 · Productionise "Two things to say. Making the association eager isn't a fix: it loads the graph everywhere, and can still be N plus one. And JOIN FETCH on a collection with pagination makes Hibernate page in memory, so for paged lists I fetch IDs first or use batch size."
Close "Fetch what the use case needs in one or two statements, and lock it in with a query-count test."

stages.name: Name it
stages.claim: one query, then one per row
stages.html:
Prove it — a plain-Java analogue with a query counter (JDK 25):

import java.util.*;
class Demo {
    static int queries = 0;
    static List<Integer> findOrders() { queries++; return List.of(1, 2, 3, 4, 5); }           // 1 query
    static List<String> itemsOf(int orderId) { queries++; return List.of("item"); }           // 1 query per order
    static Map<Integer, List<String>> itemsOfAll(List<Integer> ids) { queries++;              // 1 query for all
        Map<Integer, List<String>> m = new HashMap<>(); ids.forEach(i -> m.put(i, List.of("item"))); return m; }
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        for (int id : findOrders()) itemsOf(id);               // lazy association touched in a loop
        System.out.println("lazy in a loop: " + queries + " queries");
        queries = 0;
        itemsOfAll(findOrders());                              // what JOIN FETCH or a batch does
        System.out.println("fetched together: " + queries + " queries");
    }
}
// → lazy in a loop: 6 queries
// → fetched together: 2 queries

SELECT * FROM orders;                              -- 1 query, N rows
SELECT * FROM order_items WHERE order_id = 1;      -- + N queries, one per order,
SELECT * FROM order_items WHERE order_id = 2;      --   fired when the loop touches order.getItems()
...
Why it happens:association is LAZYthe collection is a proxyfirst access inside a loopone SELECT per parent

stages.name: Rule out the fakes
stages.claim: other reasons for a slow page
stages.html:
Fake How it differs
one slow query a single long statement in the log
missing index few statements, each slow; the plan shows a scan
too many rows fetched one statement returning far more than the page shows
connection-pool wait time passes before the first statement

stages.name: Confirm with evidence
stages.html:
Observation Likely cause Next action
statement count grows with the number of rows on the page N+1 fetch the association with the parents
many identical SELECT … WHERE parent_id = ? lazy collection touched in a loop, a mapper or a JSON serialiser find the access; fetch up front
queries fire while the response is being serialised open-session-in-view is hiding it turn OSIV off; return DTOs
the count is constant but one statement is slow not N+1 look at the plan

Tools: spring.jpa.properties.hibernate.generate_statistics=true, a datasource proxy that counts statements, or the APM's per-request span count.

stages.name: Fix by experiment
stages.html:
Experiment 1

JOIN FETCH or an entity graph

I'd load parents and the needed association in one statement.

@EntityGraph(attributePaths = "items")
List<Order> findByCustomerId(long customerId);          // or: select o from Order o join fetch o.items where …

Why? One round trip, and the fetch plan belongs to this query, not to the mapping.

Best suited when one collection is needed and the result isn't paginated.

Experiment 2

Batch fetching

I'd set @BatchSize(size = 50) or hibernate.default_batch_fetch_size.

Why? Lazy loads are grouped: WHERE order_id IN (?, ?, …). N+1 becomes 1 + N/50.

Best suited when paginating, or when several collections are needed.

Experiment 3

A DTO projection

I'd select exactly the columns into a record.

Why? No entities, no lazy proxies, no dirty checking: the cheapest read.

Best suited when the endpoint only reads.

stages.name: Validate
stages.html:
@Test
void listingOrdersUsesAConstantNumberOfQueries() {
    statistics.clear();
    service.listOrders(customerId);                               // 20 orders in the fixture
    assertThat(statistics.getPrepareStatementCount()).isLessThanOrEqualTo(2);
}
Metric Before After
statements per request 1 + N 1 or 2
p95 latency of the endpoint measure measure
rows and columns transferred measure measure

stages.name: Productionise
stages.claim: the two traps and the guards
stages.html:
Trap What happens Instead
FetchType.EAGER the association loads on every query everywhere; JPQL queries still issue it per row keep LAZY; choose the fetch per query
JOIN FETCH a collection + pagination Hibernate fetches everything and paginates in memory, with a warning page the IDs first, then fetch by ID; or use batch size
JOIN FETCH two collections a Cartesian product, or MultipleBagFetchException fetch one, batch the other
open-session-in-view left on lazy loads happen during rendering, unnoticed disable it; map to DTOs in the service
Guards:query-count assertions for hot use casesfail on the in-memory pagination warning (hibernate.query.fail_on_pagination_over_collection_fetch=true)statement count per request in dashboards

followUps.question: Entity graph or JOIN FETCH?
followUps.html:
The same result; they differ in where the fetch plan is written.

JOIN FETCH @EntityGraph
Where in the JPQL on the repository method
Works with derived queries no yes
Reusable across queries no yes, as a named graph

followUps.question: "Make the association EAGER and the problem goes away."
followUps.html:
It moves the cost to every query and often keeps the N+1.

  • Every load of the parent now loads the children, needed or not.
  • A JPQL query for parents still loads eager associations with one select each.
  • LAZY plus a per-query fetch plan is the fix.

followUps.question: The page shows 20 orders with items, and there are 2 million orders.
followUps.html:
Two steps.

query 1: select the 20 order IDs with LIMIT and OFFSET (or keyset) ─▶ query 2: select those orders join fetch items where id in (…)

Pagination happens in SQL, the collection is fetched without a row explosion.

followUps.question: Where else does N+1 hide?
followUps.html:
Anywhere a loop makes a remote call per element.

  • @ManyToOne on each row of a list (the parent side).
  • A mapper or JSON serialiser walking lazy associations.
  • REST or gRPC calls per item: the same shape outside the database.

followUps.question: How do you stop it reappearing across a team?
followUps.html:
Make it visible in tests and in telemetry.

  • Query-count assertions in integration tests of list endpoints.
  • OSIV off so lazy access outside a transaction fails loudly.
  • A dashboard and alert on statements per request.

dontSay: "Use EAGER."
"Just add JOIN FETCH" to a paginated collection query.
"It was fine in dev."

java-spring-q29.testing: whether you identify the kind of OOM first, prove a leak with the live set after full GC, and use a heap dump to find the owner.
java-spring-q29.spoken:
Beat Say
1 · Name it "First I ask which out-of-memory it is. The message says: Java heap space, Metaspace, direct buffer memory, unable to create native thread, or the container killed the process with no Java error at all. Each has a different cause."
2 · Rule out the fakes "Then I separate a leak from an undersized heap or a load-driven spike. A leak means the memory still in use after a full collection keeps rising. If it returns to the same floor each time, it is pressure, not a leak."
3 · Confirm with evidence "For a heap leak I take a heap dump, ideally the automatic one at the moment of failure, and open it in a memory analyser. The dominator tree shows which objects retain the most, and the path to GC roots shows who is holding them."
4 · Fix by experiment "The usual owners are an unbounded cache or map, a thread-local that isn't cleared on a pooled thread, listeners that are registered and never removed, and class loaders retained across redeploys. The fix is to bound or release at that owner."
5 · Validate "I validate by watching the post-full-GC live set stay flat over more than two days."
6 · Productionise "And I leave heap-dump-on-OOM enabled and alert on the live-set trend, so the next one is caught in hours."
Close "Kind of OOM, leak or pressure, heap dump, owner, bound it: bigger heap only buys days."

stages.name: Name it
stages.html:
Message or symptom Region Typical cause
Java heap space heap retained objects: caches, collections, sessions
GC overhead limit exceeded heap almost full; the collector runs constantly
Metaspace class metadata class-loader leak, runaway class generation
Direct buffer memory off-heap NIO buffers not released; too small a MaxDirectMemorySize
unable to create native thread OS threads unbounded thread creation; process limits
container OOMKilled, no Java exception whole process heap + metaspace + threads + native memory exceed the container limit

stages.name: Rule out the fakes
stages.html:
Pattern Meaning Action
post-GC floor rises steadily leak heap dump
floor flat, peaks touch the limit under load heap too small, or allocation spikes size the heap; reduce allocation
sudden jump, then OOM one huge request or query result find the request; cap result sizes

stages.name: Confirm with evidence
stages.html:
-XX:+HeapDumpOnOutOfMemoryError -XX:HeapDumpPath=/dumps     # always on
jcmd <pid> GC.heap_info                                    # live triage
jcmd <pid> GC.class_histogram                              # instances by class, live objects
jcmd <pid> JFR.start duration=120s filename=/dumps/leak.jfr
In the analyser:open the dumpdominator treelargest retained sizepath to GC rootsthe field that holds it
Observation in the dump Likely cause Next action
one HashMap or ConcurrentHashMap retains most of the heap an unbounded cache or registry bound it, add expiry
many objects reachable from Thread → threadLocals a ThreadLocal not removed on pooled threads remove() in finally
growing lists of listeners or callbacks registered, never unregistered unregister on close
several copies of the application's classes, each with its own class loader class-loader leak on redeploy find the static reference holding the old loader
millions of session or request objects sessions never expire; a queue with no consumer timeouts; bounded queue

stages.name: Fix by experiment
stages.html:
Experiment 1

Bound the cache

I'd replace the map with a size- and time-bounded cache.

Why? A map used as a cache with no eviction is the most common owner.

Best suited when the dominator is a map keyed by request data, user or tenant.

Experiment 2

Clear thread-locals

I'd wrap the usage in try/finally with remove().

Why? Pooled threads live for the life of the process, and so does anything left in their thread-locals.

Best suited when retained objects hang off worker threads.

Experiment 3

Cap what one request can load

I'd paginate or stream the query and cap collection sizes.

Why? A single unbounded result set can fill the heap without any leak.

Best suited when the growth is in steps tied to specific requests.

stages.name: Validate
stages.html:
Metric Before After
heap after full GC, trend over 3+ days rising flat
time between restarts about 2 days none
size of the suspect structure (a gauge) growing bounded
GC pause time and frequency rising steady

A soak test at production-like load reproduces a two-day leak in hours if the allocation pattern is right.

stages.name: Productionise
stages.html:
Guard Catches
heap dump on OOM, to a volume that survives the pod evidence at the moment of failure
GC logging always on (-Xlog:gc*) the post-GC trend
alert on live-set growth and on GC time share a leak within hours
gauges on every cache and queue size which structure is growing
container memory = heap + metaspace + threads + direct + headroom avoids OOMKilled with a healthy heap

followUps.question: The pod is OOMKilled but the heap never fills. Why?
followUps.html:
The process uses more than the heap.

container limit ≥ heap (-Xmx) + metaspace + thread stacks + direct buffers + code cache + GC and native overhead

Use -XX:MaxRAMPercentage with headroom, and Native Memory Tracking to see the parts.

followUps.question: "Double -Xmx."
followUps.html:
For a leak that changes two days into four.

Action Result
bigger heap longer until the same failure, and longer GC pauses on the way
find the owner the growth stops

A temporary increase is fine as mitigation while diagnosing; it isn't the diagnosis.

followUps.question: You can't take a heap dump: it's 30 GB and pauses the service.
followUps.html:
Use cheaper evidence first.

  • Class histogram twice, an hour apart: which classes grow.
  • JFR with old-object sampling: allocation sites of long-lived objects.
  • Dump one replica taken out of rotation.

followUps.question: How does a ThreadLocal leak?
followUps.html:
The value is reachable from the thread, and pooled threads never die.

request sets the thread-localrequest ends without remove()thread returns to the poolthe value stays, and so does everything it references

followUps.question: What do you tell stakeholders while it's still happening?
followUps.html:
Mitigation now, diagnosis with a date.

Now Next
scheduled rolling restarts before the failure point; a larger heap as a buffer heap dump captured, owner identified, fix and a soak test, with an estimate

dontSay: "Increase the heap."
"It's a memory leak" before checking the post-GC trend.
"Java has garbage collection, so it can't leak."

java-spring-q30.testing: whether you choose a collector from the workload's pause and throughput needs, and tune from GC logs instead of copied flags.
java-spring-q30.trap: a list of flags from a blog post with no GC log behind them.
java-spring-q30.spoken:
Beat Say
1 · Frame the axis "Collectors trade three things: pause time, throughput, and memory overhead. I pick by which one the workload can't give up."
2 · Where G1 fits "G1 is the default and the right start for most services. It divides the heap into regions, collects the ones with most garbage first, and works toward a pause-time target I set."
3 · Where ZGC fits "ZGC and Shenandoah do almost all their work concurrently with the application, so pauses stay around a millisecond or less even on very large heaps. The price is some throughput and more memory headroom. I'd choose one for a latency-sensitive service with a large heap."
4 · The deciding question "So I ask: what is the pause budget at p99, how big is the heap, and is this a latency service or a throughput batch? For batch throughput, Parallel is still the right answer; for a tiny container, Serial."
5 · What I'd tune "Then I tune little, and from evidence. Heap size first, with headroom. The pause target for G1. And before any flag, the allocation rate: creating less garbage beats any collector setting. I change one thing at a time and read the GC log before and after."
Close "G1 by default, ZGC for low-pause large heaps, and tune size and target from the log, not flags from a blog."

stages.name: Frame the axis
stages.html:
Collector Optimises Pauses Costs Typical fit
Serial footprint stop-the-world, single thread long pauses on big heaps tiny containers, one core
Parallel throughput stop-the-world, many threads pauses grow with the heap batch jobs
G1 (default) balance, with a pause target short, mostly young and mixed collections some overhead for remembered sets most services
ZGC, Shenandoah pause time sub-millisecond to a few ms, independent of heap size lower throughput, more headroom needed latency-sensitive, large heaps

stages.name: Where G1 fits
stages.html:
A G1 cycle:young collectionsheap occupancy crosses a thresholdconcurrent markingmixed collections reclaim the old regions with most garbagerepeat
Idea Meaning
regions the heap is many equal blocks; each is eden, survivor, old or humongous
garbage first collect the regions that free the most for the least work
pause target (-XX:MaxGCPauseMillis, default 200) G1 sizes each collection to try to meet it
humongous objects objects over half a region get special handling; many of them hurt

stages.name: Where ZGC fits
stages.html:
Property Detail
concurrent marking and relocation application threads keep running while objects are moved
pause independent of heap size the stop-the-world parts are tiny and constant
generational ZGC the default mode from JDK 23; it handles high allocation rates much better
cost barriers on object access reduce throughput somewhat; needs spare memory and CPU to keep up

Failure mode: if allocation outpaces the concurrent collector, threads stall waiting for memory ("allocation stall"). The fix is more headroom or less allocation.

stages.name: The deciding question
stages.html:
Workload Choice
typical web service, heap up to tens of GB, p99 budget in tens of ms G1
latency-critical (trading, real-time APIs), or very large heap ZGC
batch or analytics, throughput is everything Parallel
small container, under about 2 GB, one or two cores Serial (the JVM may select it automatically)
don't know yet G1, then measure

stages.name: What I'd tune
stages.html:
Order Lever Why
1 GC logging on (-Xlog:gc*:file=…) no tuning without evidence
2 allocation rate fewer short-lived objects, less boxing, reuse of buffers: the biggest lever
3 heap size (-Xms = -Xmx, or MaxRAMPercentage in containers) too small causes frequent collections; headroom matters most for concurrent collectors
4 pause target for G1 lower target means more, smaller collections
5 collector choice only if the pause budget still isn't met
last individual flags one at a time, each justified by a line in the log
Read in the GC log Tells you
pause times and their percentiles whether the budget is met
heap after collection, over time the live set, and whether it leaks
allocation rate pressure on the young generation
promotion rate; full GCs objects living too long; undersized heap
time share spent in GC throughput lost

Evaluation hook: p99 request latency and GC time share on a production-like load test, before and after each change.

followUps.question: Why does the generational hypothesis matter?
followUps.html:
Most objects die young, so collecting the young area often is cheap.

Area Collected Cost driven by
young frequently survivors, which are few
old rarely the live set

followUps.question: "Here are the fifteen flags we use on every service."
followUps.html:
Flags are a response to a measurement on one workload.

  • Defaults are tuned by the JVM authors for general use.
  • A copied flag may fight the collector's own heuristics.
  • Start from defaults, change one thing, compare logs.

followUps.question: A full GC with G1 takes eight seconds.
followUps.html:
Full GC is G1's fallback when it couldn't reclaim concurrently in time.

Cause Fix
heap too small for the live set more heap
marking starts too late lower the initiating occupancy; reduce allocation
many humongous allocations larger region size; avoid huge arrays
a leak fix the leak

followUps.question: How should the heap be set in a container?
followUps.html:
As a share of the limit, leaving room for everything that isn't heap.

-XX:MaxRAMPercentage=70–75        ← the rest: metaspace, thread stacks, direct buffers, GC structures

followUps.question: When is GC tuning the wrong project?
followUps.html:
When the pauses aren't what users feel.

Symptom Real cause more often
p99 latency spikes lock contention, pool waits, slow queries
high GC time wasteful allocation in a hot path

I'd confirm GC is on the latency path, with the log and a trace, before spending a sprint on it.

dontSay: "ZGC is always best."
"Set Xms, Xmx, NewRatio, SurvivorRatio…" with no log.
"GC tuning will fix our latency" before checking that GC causes it.

links.label: Low Pause Collectors ZGC and Shenandoah

java-spring-q31.testing: whether you size the pool from the database's capacity and the pod count, and treat hold time as the real lever.
java-spring-q31.trap: growing the pool to fix latency caused by long-held connections.
java-spring-q31.spoken:
Beat Say
1 · Clarify "Smaller than most people expect. I'd ask how many cores the database has, how many application instances connect, and how long a request holds a connection."
2 · Constraints and numbers "The pool is bounded by what the database can execute at once, which is about its core count, not by how many request threads I have. And the real load is pool size times instances: twenty connections on fifteen pods is three hundred connections to one database."
3 · Baseline design "So I start small, around ten per instance, with a connection timeout of a second or two so callers fail fast, and leak detection enabled. Then I measure wait time and active connections under load."
4 · Deep-dive the hard part "The lever that matters is hold time. If each request holds a connection for two hundred milliseconds, ten connections serve fifty requests a second. Hold it across a remote call, or an LLM call that takes five seconds, and the same pool serves two."
5 · Failure modes "An undersized pool and a leak look identical: connection-timeout errors under load. I tell them apart by whether active connections return to zero when traffic stops."
6 · Evolve "At scale I put a pooler such as PgBouncer in front, and keep transactions short."
Close "Size to the database, multiply by pods, fail fast, and shorten the hold time."

stages.name: Clarify
stages.html:
Ask Why
database cores and its max_connections the ceiling the whole fleet shares
number of application instances, including during a rollout the multiplier
connection hold time per request decides throughput per connection
other clients of the same database jobs, migrations, analysts also take connections

stages.name: Constraints and numbers
stages.html:
real connections   = pool size × instances                      20 × 15 pods = 300          (illustrative)
during a rollout   = pool size × (instances + surge)            20 × 20      = 400
starting point     ≈ (database cores × 2) + effective spindles  for the WHOLE fleet, then divided by instances
                     (the guideline from the HikariCP wiki, originally from PostgreSQL)
Belief Reality
"more connections, more throughput" past the database's cores, queries just queue inside the database, with more context switching
"pool size should match the thread count" most of a request isn't spent in the database
"each pod needs 50" fifteen pods then open 750 connections

stages.name: Baseline design
stages.html:
spring.datasource.hikari.maximum-pool-size=10
spring.datasource.hikari.connection-timeout=2000          # ms: fail fast instead of queueing for 30 s
spring.datasource.hikari.leak-detection-threshold=5000    # ms: log a stack trace if held longer
spring.datasource.hikari.max-lifetime=1800000             # shorter than any database or proxy idle timeout
Setting Purpose
maximumPoolSize the cap; with HikariCP a fixed-size pool is the recommended mode
connectionTimeout how long a thread waits for a connection before an error
leakDetectionThreshold names the code that held a connection too long
maxLifetime retire connections before the network or database drops them

stages.name: Deep-dive the hard part
stages.html:
throughput per pool ≈ pool size / hold time
10 connections / 0.2 s   = 50 requests per second
10 connections / 5 s     =  2 requests per second       ← a connection held across an LLM or HTTP call
Wrong:begin transactionquerycall remote serviceupdatecommit
Right:querycommitcall remote servicebeginupdatecommit
Hold-time offender Fix
@Transactional around a remote call move the call outside the transaction
open-session-in-view the connection is held for the whole request, including rendering: turn it off
REQUIRES_NEW two connections per thread: count them
streaming a large result set slowly paginate, or a dedicated pool for reports
N+1 many round trips while holding the connection

stages.name: Failure modes
stages.html:
Observation Likely cause Next action
timeouts under load; active returns to 0 when idle pool too small for the hold time shorten hold time first, then resize
active stays high with no traffic a leak: connections never returned leak detection stack trace; find the missing close
database CPU saturated, many active sessions too many connections fleet-wide reduce pool size; add a pooler
errors right after a rollout begins old and new pods together exceed max_connections budget for surge; lower per-pod size
first request after idle fails a connection killed by a firewall or the database maxLifetime and keepalive below that timeout

stages.name: Evolve
stages.html:
Step When
an external pooler (PgBouncer in transaction mode, RDS Proxy) many instances or serverless functions share one database
separate pools for interactive requests and for batch or reporting a slow report must not starve the API
read replicas with their own pool read-heavy load
metrics: active, idle, pending threads, acquisition time, timeouts always; alert on pending > 0 for long

Evaluation hook: p95 connection-acquisition time under a load test at peak concurrency.

followUps.question: Why can a smaller pool be faster?
followUps.html:
The database runs about as many queries in parallel as it has cores; the rest only contend.

Pool total Database behaviour
≈ cores each query runs; others wait cheaply in the pool
far above cores context switching, lock and cache contention inside the database

followUps.question: "We're getting connection timeouts, raise the pool to 100."
followUps.html:
That moves the queue into the database and hides the cause.

  • Check hold time and leaks first.
  • Multiply by pods before changing anything.
  • A larger pool can turn slow requests into a database outage.

followUps.question: With virtual threads, thousands of requests want a connection at once.
followUps.html:
The pool is now the only limiter, so make the limit deliberate.

  • Keep the pool small; virtual threads waiting for it are cheap.
  • Set the acquisition timeout so overload fails fast.
  • Add a semaphore or bulkhead if a fair queue is needed.

followUps.question: How do you measure hold time?
followUps.html:
From pool metrics and tracing.

Source Shows
HikariCP usage-time metric how long connections are out of the pool
a trace span per transaction which code path is slow
leak-detection log the stack that exceeded the threshold

followUps.question: Who owns the connection budget across teams?
followUps.html:
Whoever owns the database, as an explicit allocation.

max_connections ≥ Σ over services (pool size × max instances) + admin and migration headroom

A table of that sum, reviewed when a service scales, prevents the fleet-wide outage.

dontSay: "As big as the thread pool."
"Increase it until the errors stop."
A pool size with no mention of how many instances run.

java-spring-q32.testing: whether you understand the persistence-context boundary and reject the two popular non-fixes.
java-spring-q32.spoken:
Beat Say
1 · Name it "A lazy association is a proxy that loads its data on first access, using the persistence context it came from. That context closes when the transaction ends. The controller touched the proxy after that, so there was nothing to load it with."
2 · Rule out the wrong fixes "Two fixes make the error disappear and the design worse. Making the association eager loads it on every query, everywhere. Open-session-in-view keeps the session open for the whole request, so lazy loads run during JSON serialisation: the error goes away and N plus one and long-held connections arrive."
3 · Confirm with evidence "The stack trace shows which association was touched and where: usually the serialiser or a mapper outside the service."
4 · Fix by experiment "The right fix is to fetch what the use case needs inside the transaction: an entity graph or JOIN FETCH on that query, or a DTO projection. The cleanest design doesn't let entities leave the service at all: the service returns DTOs."
5 · Validate "I validate with a test that calls the endpoint with open-session-in-view off."
6 · Productionise "And I turn it off on purpose. Boot enables it by default; with it off, this class of bug fails loudly in development instead of quietly costing queries in production."
Close "The context ended; load inside the boundary, return DTOs, and switch OSIV off."

stages.name: Name it
stages.html:
Term Meaning
lazy proxy a placeholder that queries on first access
persistence context the session: the unit that can load and track entities
boundary by default, the transaction

stages.name: Rule out the wrong fixes
stages.html:
"Fix" What it really does Cost
FetchType.EAGER loads the association on every load of the parent over-fetching everywhere; still N+1 on queries
open-session-in-view (spring.jpa.open-in-view=true, Boot's default) keeps the session open until the response is written lazy loads during rendering: hidden N+1; a connection held for the whole request
hibernate.enable_lazy_load_no_trans opens a new session per lazy access one extra connection and transaction per access: the worst option
Hibernate.initialize() sprinkled in services forces loading works, but it is a fetch plan written by hand, one property at a time

stages.name: Confirm with evidence
stages.html:
LazyInitializationException: failed to lazily initialize a collection of role:
  com.shop.Order.items: could not initialize proxy - no Session
    at ...jackson...BeanSerializer.serialize        ← touched during JSON serialisation
Observation Likely cause Next action
trace passes through the JSON serialiser an entity returned from the controller return a DTO
trace is in a mapper called by the controller mapping happens outside the transaction map inside the service
trace is in an @Async method or another thread the entity crossed a thread boundary pass IDs or DTOs
it appeared after disabling OSIV the access was always there, now visible fix the fetch

stages.name: Fix by experiment
stages.html:
Experiment 1

A fetch plan on the query

I'd add an entity graph or a JOIN FETCH for this use case.

@EntityGraph(attributePaths = "items")
Optional<Order> findWithItemsById(long id);

Why? The association is loaded in the same statement, inside the transaction.

Best suited when the caller really needs the entity graph.

Experiment 2

Return a DTO from the service

I'd map to a record inside the transactional method.

@Transactional(readOnly = true)
OrderView getOrder(long id) { return OrderView.from(orders.findWithItemsById(id).orElseThrow()); }

Why? Nothing lazy leaves the boundary; the API shape is decoupled from the entity.

Best suited as the default for anything a controller returns.

Experiment 3

A projection query

I'd select only the needed columns straight into a record.

Why? No entities, no proxies, the cheapest read.

Best suited for read-only endpoints and lists.

stages.name: Validate
stages.html:
Check Passes when
endpoint test with spring.jpa.open-in-view=false no exception, correct body
statement count for the request constant: one or two
connection hold time ends when the service method returns

stages.name: Productionise
stages.html:
Guard Effect
spring.jpa.open-in-view=false in every environment lazy access outside a transaction is an error on day one
entities never cross the service boundary an architecture rule: controllers depend on DTOs only
LAZY on all associations (set it explicitly on @ManyToOne and @OneToOne, whose default is eager) fetch plans are per query
query-count assertions on main endpoints N+1 is caught with the same tests

Why this matters: the exception is the persistence layer telling you a fetch decision was never made. The fix is to make it.

followUps.question: Why does Boot enable OSIV by default?
followUps.html:
For beginner convenience, and it logs a warning at startup saying so.

With OSIV Without
templates and serialisers can touch lazy properties they can't, so fetching must be designed

followUps.question: "Mark the association EAGER; the exception is gone."
followUps.html:
So is your control over what each query loads.

  • Every query on the parent now pays for the children.
  • Eager can't be turned off per query; lazy can be overridden per query.

followUps.question: The service method is @Transactional and it still throws inside the service.
followUps.html:
Then the transaction isn't actually active there.

Cause Check
self-invocation the method was called through this
entity loaded in an earlier, finished transaction it is detached: reload or merge
the code runs on another thread transactions and sessions are thread-bound

followUps.question: @ManyToOne is lazy too?
followUps.html:
Only if you say so: the JPA default for to-one associations is eager.

Association JPA default
@OneToMany, @ManyToMany lazy
@ManyToOne, @OneToOne eager

followUps.question: How do you roll out "OSIV off" on a large existing application?
followUps.html:
Per environment, with tests finding the breakages first.

Plan:turn it off in testsfix endpoints that fail, adding fetch plans or DTOsturn it off in stagingwatch for the exceptionproduction

dontSay: "Make it EAGER."
"Enable open-session-in-view."
"Call getItems().size() in the service to initialise it" as the design.

java-spring-q33.testing: whether you size from the wait-to-compute ratio, bound the queue, and treat the rejection policy as a design decision.
java-spring-q33.trap: Executors.newCachedThreadPool() or an unbounded queue in production.
java-spring-q33.spoken:
Beat Say
1 · Clarify "I'd ask what the tasks do: compute, or mostly wait on I/O. And what should happen to work that arrives when everything is busy."
2 · Constraints and numbers "For CPU-bound work, about one thread per core. For I/O-bound work, cores times one plus the ratio of wait time to compute time. A task that waits ninety milliseconds and computes ten on eight cores gives about eighty threads. That's a starting point to measure, not a result."
3 · Baseline design "I build a ThreadPoolExecutor explicitly: fixed core and max, a bounded queue, named threads, and a chosen rejection policy."
4 · Deep-dive the hard part "When it's full, meaning all threads busy and the queue at capacity, the rejection handler runs. Abort throws, so the caller fails fast. Caller-runs executes the task on the submitting thread, which slows the producer: natural backpressure. Discard drops work silently. In a small test, two threads and a queue of two accept four tasks and reject the next two."
5 · Failure modes "An unbounded queue never rejects: it turns overload into growing latency and then an out-of-memory error. A cached pool creates threads without limit."
6 · Evolve "I give each downstream dependency its own pool, as a bulkhead, and expose queue depth and rejections as metrics."
Close "Size from wait over compute, bound the queue, choose the rejection, and isolate by dependency."

stages.name: Clarify
stages.claim: what the tasks do, and what overload should do
stages.html:
Ask Why
CPU-bound or I/O-bound? decides the formula
how long does a task wait and compute? the ratio sizes the pool
can work be dropped, delayed, or must it be refused? decides queue and rejection policy
what limits the thing the tasks call? a pool larger than the downstream capacity only moves the queue

stages.name: Constraints and numbers
stages.html:
CPU-bound:   threads ≈ cores  (+1)
I/O-bound:   threads ≈ cores × (1 + wait time / compute time)

8 cores, task waits 90 ms and computes 10 ms:   8 × (1 + 90 / 10) = 80 threads
8 cores, pure computation:                      8 (or 9)
Caveat Detail
in a container, "cores" is the CPU limit not the host's core count
the downstream has its own limit 80 threads against a database pool of 10 means 70 wait
each platform thread costs stack memory hundreds are fine, tens of thousands aren't
measure utilisation, queue depth and latency under load decide the final number

stages.name: Baseline design
stages.html:
ThreadPoolExecutor pool = new ThreadPoolExecutor(
    16, 16,                                    // core = max: a fixed pool
    0, TimeUnit.SECONDS,
    new ArrayBlockingQueue<>(100),             // bounded
    Thread.ofPlatform().name("pricing-", 0).factory(),      // named threads
    new ThreadPoolExecutor.CallerRunsPolicy());             // chosen overload behaviour
Parameter Choice Why
core and max equal with a bounded queue, extra threads are only created once the queue is full, which surprises people
queue bounded overload must become visible
thread names by purpose a thread dump during an incident is readable
rejection handler explicit the default aborts; make it a decision

stages.name: Deep-dive the hard part
stages.html:
Prove it — 2 threads, queue of 2, six tasks that block (JDK 25):

import java.util.concurrent.*;
class Demo {
    public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception {
        CountDownLatch hold = new CountDownLatch(1);
        ThreadPoolExecutor pool = new ThreadPoolExecutor(2, 2, 0, TimeUnit.SECONDS,
            new ArrayBlockingQueue<>(2), new ThreadPoolExecutor.AbortPolicy());   // 2 threads + 2 queued = 4
        int accepted = 0, rejected = 0;
        for (int i = 0; i < 6; i++) {
            try { pool.execute(() -> { try { hold.await(); } catch (InterruptedException e) { } }); accepted++; }
            catch (RejectedExecutionException e) { rejected++; }
        }
        System.out.println("accepted " + accepted + ", rejected " + rejected);
        System.out.println("running " + pool.getActiveCount() + ", queued " + pool.getQueue().size());
        hold.countDown(); pool.shutdown();
    }
}
// → accepted 4, rejected 2
// → running 2, queued 2
Order of filling:core threadsqueueextra threads up to maxrejection handler
Policy On overload Use when
AbortPolicy (default) throws RejectedExecutionException callers can fail fast and report it
CallerRunsPolicy the submitting thread runs the task slowing the producer is acceptable: backpressure
DiscardPolicy drops the new task silently loss is acceptable (sampling, best-effort metrics)
DiscardOldestPolicy drops the oldest queued task newest data matters most

stages.name: Failure modes
stages.html:
Construct Hidden behaviour Failure
Executors.newFixedThreadPool(n) an unbounded LinkedBlockingQueue queue grows until out-of-memory; latency grows first
Executors.newCachedThreadPool() unbounded thread creation thousands of threads under a burst; native memory exhausted
one shared pool for everything no isolation one slow dependency occupies every thread
CallerRuns on a request thread pool the web server's own threads do the work acceptable backpressure, or a stall, depending on what they run
tasks that submit to their own pool and wait thread starvation deadlock separate pools, or don't block on sub-tasks

stages.name: Evolve
stages.html:
Step Why
a pool per downstream dependency a slow payment provider can't consume the threads the search calls need
metrics: active threads, queue depth, completed, rejected queue depth rising is the early warning
timeouts on every task a hung call would hold a thread for ever
graceful shutdown: shutdown(), then awaitTermination in-flight work finishes on deploy
virtual threads for blocking I/O (JDK 21+) no pool sizing; limit concurrency with a semaphore instead

Thread-safety: tasks share nothing mutable unless it is thread-safe; results come back through futures.

followUps.question: Why doesn't the pool grow before the queue fills?
followUps.html:
That is how ThreadPoolExecutor is specified: queue first, then extra threads.

State Action on a new task
fewer than core threads start a thread
core busy, queue has room enqueue
queue full, below max start a thread
queue full, at max reject

followUps.question: "Use newCachedThreadPool, it scales automatically."
followUps.html:
It scales without limit.

  • A burst of 10,000 slow tasks creates 10,000 threads.
  • Bounded pool + bounded queue + policy is the production shape.

followUps.question: 🧪 Core 4, max 8, queue 10, and 20 blocking tasks arrive at once.
followUps.html:
18 are accepted, 2 are rejected.

4 run on core threads + 10 queued + 4 more threads (up to max 8) = 18 accepted;  20 − 18 = 2 rejected

followUps.question: How do you size it in a container with a 2-CPU limit on a 64-core node?
followUps.html:
From the limit: the JVM reports 2 available processors.

  • Modern JVMs are container-aware; Runtime.availableProcessors() returns the limit.
  • Check with -XX:ActiveProcessorCount if it must be forced.

followUps.question: When is the answer "no thread pool"?
followUps.html:
For blocking I/O on a current JDK, and for work that belongs in a queue.

Situation Alternative
many blocking calls one virtual thread per task, with a semaphore for limits
work that must survive a restart a durable message queue with consumers

dontSay: "Executors.newFixedThreadPool is bounded" — its queue isn't.
"More threads, more throughput."
"When it's full, tasks wait" — only if the queue is unbounded, which is the bug.

java-spring-q34.testing: whether you know context propagation is the whole problem, and where it silently breaks: threads and queues.
java-spring-q34.trap: losing the trace at the first @Async or Kafka boundary.
java-spring-q34.spoken:
Beat Say
1 · Clarify "I'd ask which hops are HTTP and which are messaging, whether any work is asynchronous, and what volume we're tracing, since that decides sampling."
2 · Constraints and numbers "At high volume I can't keep every trace, so I sample: a small share up front for cost, and ideally tail sampling that keeps every trace with an error or high latency."
3 · Baseline design "The mechanism is a trace ID created at the edge and propagated on every hop in the W3C traceparent header. Each service creates spans under it. In Spring, Micrometer Tracing with OpenTelemetry instruments the common clients and servers automatically, and puts the trace ID into the logging context so every log line carries it."
4 · Deep-dive the hard part "The hard part is the boundaries where context doesn't travel by itself. A new thread, an executor or an at-Async method loses it unless the executor propagates context. A message queue loses it unless the producer writes the header into the message and the consumer reads it."
5 · Failure modes "So a broken trace usually means a hand-built HTTP client, a custom thread pool, or a consumer that starts a fresh trace."
6 · Evolve "Then I link traces, logs and metrics by trace ID, and use span links for batch or fan-in cases where there isn't one parent."
Close "One ID at the edge, carried on every hop, in every log line, and explicitly across threads and queues."

stages.name: Clarify
stages.html:
Ask Why
HTTP, gRPC or messaging per hop? each has its own carrier for the context
any async work, thread pools, schedulers? context is thread-bound
requests per second? decides sampling
who consumes traces? on-call debugging needs errors kept; capacity work needs representative samples

stages.name: Constraints and numbers
stages.html:
traceparent: 00-4bf92f3577b34da6a3ce929d0e0e4736-00f067aa0ba902b7-01
             │  └ trace-id (32 hex): the same on every hop     │           └ flags: 01 = sampled
             └ version                                         └ parent span id (16 hex): changes per hop
Sampling Decides Trade
head (at the edge, by probability) before the request runs cheap; may drop the one failing trace
tail (in a collector, after the trace completes) with full knowledge keeps errors and slow traces; needs buffering

stages.name: Baseline design
stages.html:
Piece In a Spring Boot 3 service
instrumentation Micrometer Observation + Micrometer Tracing, bridged to OpenTelemetry
HTTP in and out auto-instrumented server, RestClient, WebClient (when built from the auto-configured builders)
logs trace and span IDs placed in the MDC and printed by the log pattern
export OTLP to a collector, then to the tracing backend

stages.name: Deep-dive the hard part
stages.html:
Boundary Why it breaks Fix
@Async, custom executors, CompletableFuture the context lives in a thread-local of the calling thread a context-propagating task decorator or executor wrapper
message queues (Kafka, RabbitMQ, SQS) there is no HTTP header producer injects into message headers; consumer extracts and continues
hand-built HTTP clients (new RestTemplate(), raw HttpClient) not instrumented use the injected builder, or add the interceptor
reactive pipelines execution hops threads Reactor context propagation enabled
scheduled jobs and batch no incoming request start a new trace per run; link to causes
third-party or legacy hops they drop unknown headers wrap at the edge; correlate by a business ID
Wrong:request threadexecutor.submit(task)task logs with no trace ID
Right:request threadcontext-propagating executortask runs as a child span

stages.name: Failure modes
stages.html:
Observation Likely cause Next action
trace stops at service 2; service 3 has its own new trace propagation lost on that call check the client used for that hop
logs in an async method have no trace ID executor without context propagation wrap the executor
consumer traces are unconnected to producers headers not written or not read enable observation on the messaging template and listener
most error traces are missing head sampling dropped them tail sampling, or always sample on error
spans exist but timings look wrong clock skew, or missing spans for a slow section add a span around the gap

stages.name: Evolve
stages.html:
Addition Gives
trace ID in every log line and in error responses from a user's error to the trace in one step
exemplars on metrics from a latency spike to an example trace
span links batch jobs, fan-in, and consumers that process many messages in one go
baggage, sparingly tenant or user ID carried along; never secrets
a correlation ID from the client as well ties retries and user actions together

Evaluation hook: a synthetic request through all five services whose trace must be complete: an automated check that propagation still works after each release.

followUps.question: Trace ID or correlation ID?
followUps.html:
Both: they answer different questions.

Trace ID Correlation ID
Scope one request's path through the system one business action, across retries and requests
Created by the tracing library the client or the edge

followUps.question: "Auto-instrumentation handles it all."
followUps.html:
It handles the clients and servers it knows, on the threads it sees.

  • Custom executors, hand-built clients and custom protocols aren't covered.
  • Those are exactly where traces break.

followUps.question: A consumer processes a batch of 500 messages from 500 different traces.
followUps.html:
There is no single parent, so use links.

one batch spanspan links to each message's originating traceper-message child spans where needed

followUps.question: What goes in a span, and what must not?
followUps.html:
Low-cardinality names, useful attributes, no secrets.

Put in Keep out
operation name, status, route template, tenant tokens, passwords, raw personal data, full request bodies

followUps.question: What does tracing cost, and who pays?
followUps.html:
CPU and network per span, plus storage; sampling is the budget control.

Lever Effect
sampling rate and tail policies storage and backend cost
span count per request overhead in each service
retention period storage

I'd set a per-service budget and keep 100% of error traces.

dontSay: "We log a request ID" — in which services, and across threads?
"OpenTelemetry does it automatically."
"We trace everything at 100%" at high volume.

java-spring-q35.testing: whether you reach for a saga with compensations, an outbox for atomic publish, and idempotent consumers, and state the consistency the user sees meanwhile.
java-spring-q35.trap: proposing distributed two-phase commit, or describing only the happy path.
java-spring-q35.spoken:
Beat Say
1 · Clarify "I'd ask what the steps are, which can be undone, and what the user sees meanwhile. Say: create order, reserve stock, take payment."
2 · Constraints and numbers "Each service owns its database, so there is no shared transaction. Two-phase commit across them would couple their availability and hold locks across the network. So I accept eventual consistency and design for it."
3 · Baseline design "The pattern is a saga: a sequence of local transactions, each with a compensating action that undoes it semantically. If payment fails, release the stock and cancel the order. I'd use orchestration: one coordinator holds the saga's state and tells each service what to do, so the flow is visible in one place."
4 · Deep-dive the hard part "The hard part is making 'update my database and publish the event' atomic. That is the outbox pattern: in the same local transaction I write the business row and an outbox row. A relay, or change-data-capture, publishes outbox rows to the broker afterwards. Delivery is at least once, so every consumer is idempotent: it records the message ID and ignores repeats."
5 · Failure modes "Failures I plan for: a compensation that itself fails, so it retries until done; steps that can't be undone, which go last; and stuck sagas, which need a timeout and an alert."
6 · Evolve "Later, a durable workflow engine replaces the hand-built orchestrator."
Close "Local transactions with compensations, an outbox for atomic publish, idempotent consumers, and an honest pending state."

stages.name: Clarify
stages.claim: steps, reversibility, what the user sees
stages.html:
Ask Why
what are the steps and who owns each? one local transaction per service
which steps can be compensated? a refund undoes a charge; an email can't be unsent
what is the user shown in between? "order pending" is part of the design
how long may it take? seconds allow a synchronous feel; minutes need status polling or notifications

stages.name: Constraints and numbers
stages.html:
Two-phase commit (XA) Saga
Consistency atomic across services eventual, with compensations
Availability every participant and the coordinator must be up each step proceeds independently
Locks held across network round trips local and short
Support many brokers and cloud databases don't offer it works with any database and broker
Isolation yes none between steps: other requests can see intermediate state 
availability of a 3-party atomic commit ≈ 0.999 × 0.999 × 0.999 ≈ 0.997      (illustrative per-service availability)

stages.name: Baseline design
stages.html:
Orchestration Choreography
Control a coordinator sends commands each service reacts to events
Flow visible in one state machine the topology of subscriptions
Coupling services depend on the coordinator's commands services depend on each other's events
Pick when more than two or three steps, or compensations a short, stable chain
Step Local transaction Compensation
1 order created as PENDING mark CANCELLED
2 stock reserved release reservation
3 payment charged refund
end order CONFIRMED —

stages.name: Deep-dive the hard part
stages.html:
The dual-write problem:commit to the databasecrashevent never published (or published, then the commit fails)
Outbox:one local transaction writes the business row and an outbox rowrelay or CDC reads the outboxpublishes to the brokermarks it sent
@Transactional
void reserve(ReserveStock cmd) {
