stages.name: Failure modes
stages.claim: the unhappy paths are the design
stages.html:
Failure Symptom Control
a compensation fails saga stuck half undone compensations are idempotent and retried until they succeed; alert after N attempts
a step can't be compensated (shipment dispatched, email sent) no undo exists order steps so irreversible ones come last, after everything that can fail
a reply never arrives saga waits for ever timeout per step, then compensate or query status
duplicate or out-of-order messages double charge, release before reserve idempotency keys; state checks before acting
no isolation a user sees stock reserved for an order that is later cancelled semantic locks: a PENDING state others respect
orchestrator crashes mid-saga flow lost saga state persisted; resume on restart

stages.name: Evolve
stages.html:
Step Gives
a workflow engine (for example Temporal or Camunda) persisted state, timers, retries and compensations as code
a saga-state table and dashboard which sagas are in which step, and how long
change-data-capture for the outbox (for example Debezium) no polling relay to run
reconciliation job finds orders stuck in PENDING and repairs them
What the user sees:"Order received, confirming payment"confirmed or cancelled, with a notification. Saying that sentence is part of the answer.

followUps.question: Why not just publish the event after the commit?
followUps.html:
A crash between the two loses the event.

Order Failure window
commit, then publish crash after commit: state changed, nobody told
publish, then commit commit fails: event describes something that didn't happen
outbox none: both are one transaction

followUps.question: "Use a distributed transaction with XA across the three services."
followUps.html:
It ties three services' availability together and most modern infrastructure doesn't support it.

  • Locks held across the network while waiting for the slowest participant.
  • A failed coordinator leaves participants in doubt.
  • Sagas trade atomicity for availability, deliberately.

followUps.question: The payment was charged, and the "charged" reply was lost.
followUps.html:
The orchestrator retries the charge with the same idempotency key.

retry charge(sagaId)payment service finds the keyreturns the original resultno second charge

followUps.question: Is a compensation the same as a rollback?
followUps.html:
No: it is a new forward action that semantically undoes the earlier one.

Rollback Compensation
the change never became visible the change was visible; a refund, release or cancellation follows

followUps.question: How do you know sagas are healthy in production?
followUps.html:
By watching time in state and the outbox backlog.

  • Sagas older than their expected duration, per step.
  • Outbox rows unsent and their age.
  • Compensation rate per step: a rising rate points at the failing dependency.

dontSay: "Wrap it in a distributed transaction."
"Publish an event after saving" — with no outbox.
A saga with no compensations and no timeout.

java-spring-q36.testing: whether you layer timeout, circuit breaker, bulkhead and bounded retry in the right order, with an explicit fallback.
java-spring-q36.trap: retries without a breaker: a self-inflicted denial of service.
java-spring-q36.spoken:
Beat Say
1 · Clarify "I'd ask how A fails today: do its threads pile up waiting on B until A itself stops answering? That is the cascade. And what A should return when B is unavailable."
2 · Constraints and numbers "The mechanism is resource exhaustion. If A has two hundred request threads and each call to B hangs for thirty seconds, A is fully blocked within seconds of B going down."
3 · Baseline design "Four layers, in this order. A short timeout on every call, because without it nothing ever fails and nothing trips. A circuit breaker that opens when the failure rate crosses a threshold, so calls fail fast without touching B. A bulkhead, so calls to B have their own small pool and can't take all of A's threads. And retries only for idempotent calls, few, with backoff and jitter."
4 · Deep-dive the hard part "The breaker has three states. Closed: calls pass. Open: calls are rejected immediately for a cool-down. Half-open: a few trial calls decide whether to close again."
5 · Failure modes "The dangerous combination is retry without a breaker: every caller multiplies its traffic exactly when B is weakest. And a breaker without a fallback just changes the error."
6 · Evolve "So I define the fallback per use case: a cached value, a degraded response, or a clear fast failure."
Close "Timeout, breaker, bulkhead, bounded retry, explicit fallback: fail fast and stay up."

stages.name: Clarify
stages.claim: how A dies, and what it should return
stages.html:
Ask Why
is the call to B on the critical path? optional data can be dropped; required data needs a fallback or a fast error
is the call idempotent? decides whether retry is allowed at all
what does B's failure look like: errors or slowness? slowness is worse: it holds threads
what may A return without B? cached, partial, queued, or an honest failure

stages.name: Constraints and numbers
stages.html:
A: 200 request threads, 100 requests/s, each calls B                   (illustrative)
B hangs; no timeout → each thread blocks for 30 s
threads consumed per second = 100   →   A is fully blocked after 2 s, including endpoints that never call B
with a 500 ms timeout: at most 100 × 0.5 = 50 threads are ever waiting on B
The chain:B slowA's threads waitA's pool exhaustedA stops answeringA's callers waitthe outage spreads upward

stages.name: Baseline design
stages.html:
Around each call to B:bulkheadcircuit breakerretry (bounded)timeoutthe HTTP callfallback on any failure
Layer Purpose Without it
timeout (connect and response) bounds how long a thread waits nothing fails, so nothing else can react
circuit breaker stops calling a dependency that is failing every request still pays the timeout
bulkhead (separate pool or semaphore for B) caps how much of A can be tied up in B B's failure takes A's unrelated endpoints too
retry (idempotent only, few, with backoff and jitter) rides out a transient blip — and with it, uncontrolled: amplification
fallback defines what the caller gets the breaker just produces a different exception 
@CircuitBreaker(name = "inventory", fallbackMethod = "cachedStock")     // Resilience4j with Spring Boot
@Bulkhead(name = "inventory")
@TimeLimiter(name = "inventory")
CompletableFuture<Stock> stock(String sku) { return client.fetch(sku); }

These annotations are proxy-based, so the call must come from another bean.

stages.name: Deep-dive the hard part
stages.html:
Prove it — a minimal breaker: opens after 3 failures, cools down for 30 ticks (JDK 25):

class Demo {
    enum State { CLOSED, OPEN, HALF_OPEN }
    static State state = State.CLOSED; static int failures = 0; static long openedAt = 0;
    static String call(boolean downstreamUp, long now) {
        if (state == State.OPEN) {
            if (now - openedAt < 30) return "fail fast (no call made)";
            state = State.HALF_OPEN;                           // cool-down over: allow one probe
        }
        if (downstreamUp) { state = State.CLOSED; failures = 0; return "ok"; }
        if (state == State.HALF_OPEN || ++failures >= 3) { state = State.OPEN; openedAt = now; }
        return "error";
    }
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        for (int t = 0; t < 5; t++) System.out.println("t=" + t + " " + call(false, t) + " → " + state);
        System.out.println("t=40 " + call(true, 40) + " → " + state);
    }
}
// → t=0 error → CLOSED
// → t=1 error → CLOSED
// → t=2 error → OPEN
// → t=3 fail fast (no call made) → OPEN
// → t=4 fail fast (no call made) → OPEN
// → t=40 ok → CLOSED
Tick Event State after
0, 1 errors counted CLOSED
2 third failure OPEN
3, 4 rejected without calling B OPEN
40 cool-down over, trial call succeeds CLOSED

A production breaker uses a sliding window and a failure rate, counts slow calls as failures, and allows several trial calls.

stages.name: Failure modes
stages.html:
Failure Symptom Control
retry without a breaker traffic to B multiplies during its outage breaker outside the retry; a retry budget
retries at every layer 3 × 3 × 3 = 27 calls for one request retry at one layer only
retrying non-idempotent calls duplicate orders or payments idempotency keys, or no retry
timeout longer than the caller's own A keeps working for a client that already gave up timeouts shrink as calls go deeper (deadline propagation)
synchronised retries waves of load when B recovers jitter
one breaker for all of B's endpoints a broken endpoint blocks the healthy ones a breaker per operation or host
fallback that calls another struggling service the cascade moves sideways fallbacks must be cheap and local

stages.name: Evolve
stages.html:
Use case Fallback
product page needs stock level last cached value, marked "may be out of date"
recommendations omit the section
payment authorisation fail fast with a clear message; never guess
a write that can wait accept and queue for later processing
Operate How
breaker state as a metric and alert an open breaker is an incident signal for B's owners
load shedding at A's edge protect A itself when overloaded
chaos or game-day tests inject latency into B and confirm A stays up

Evaluation hook: with B made slow in a test environment, A's p99 for endpoints that don't use B must not move.

followUps.question: Why is the timeout the first thing?
followUps.html:
A breaker counts failures, and a call that never returns never fails.

Without a timeout With one
threads hang; the breaker sees nothing calls fail within the bound; the breaker opens

followUps.question: "Add three retries, that makes it resilient."
followUps.html:
Against a transient blip, yes. Against an outage it triples the load.

100 req/s × (1 + 3 retries) = 400 calls/s arriving at a service that is already failing

followUps.question: B isn't down, just slow at p99.
followUps.html:
Treat slow calls as failures for the breaker, and consider hedging.

  • Slow-call rate threshold on the breaker.
  • A tighter timeout with a fallback.
  • A hedged second request for idempotent reads, within a budget.

followUps.question: Thread-pool or semaphore bulkhead?
followUps.html:
A thread pool isolates and can time out; a semaphore is lighter and only limits.

Thread-pool bulkhead Semaphore bulkhead
Runs the call on its own threads the caller's thread
Can abandon a hung call yes no
Overhead higher minimal; fits virtual threads

followUps.question: Where should this live: library, sidecar or mesh?
followUps.html:
Timeouts and retries can live in a mesh; fallbacks need application knowledge.

Concern Best place
timeouts, retries, outlier ejection service mesh or client library, consistently
fallback content, idempotency application code

Whichever is chosen, configure retries in exactly one layer.

dontSay: "Add retries."
"Use a circuit breaker" with no timeout and no fallback.
"B's team should fix their service" — A must survive regardless.

java-spring-q37.testing: whether you bring the standard RAG architecture onto Spring's abstractions, and show what a Java platform already gives you.
java-spring-q37.trap: treating Spring AI as a different architecture, or proposing a Python sidecar by reflex.
java-spring-q37.spoken:
Beat Say
1 · Clarify "I'd ask what the documents are, who may see which, and how fresh answers must be."
2 · Constraints and numbers "I'd set a budget per answer for latency, context tokens and cost, and a recall target on a labelled question set."
3 · Baseline design "It is the same architecture as on the Python side, with Spring bindings: two pipelines. Ingestion is a batch job: a document reader, a text splitter, an embedding model, and a write to a VectorStore, which is an interface over pgvector, Redis, Qdrant and others. The query path uses ChatClient with a question-answer advisor that embeds the question, searches the store, and adds the retrieved chunks to the prompt before the model call."
4 · Deep-dive the hard part "The hard part is the same as everywhere: retrieval quality and the contract between the two pipelines. The embedding model, the chunking scheme and the index are one versioned unit; change one and you re-embed. And access control must be applied as a metadata filter at search time, from the authenticated user, not from the prompt."
5 · Failure modes "Failures: ingestion inside a request, a model swap that mixes embeddings, a connection held across the LLM call, and unfiltered retrieval."
6 · Evolve "What Java adds is everything around it that already exists: security, transactions, observability, deployment. Then hybrid search, reranking and an evaluation set in CI."
Close "Same RAG design, Spring abstractions, and the platform's existing security and operations around it."

who may see what metadata on every chunk, filters on every search

latency and volume model choice, streaming, caching
must answers cite sources return chunk IDs with the answer

index version = embedding model + its version + chunking scheme + metadata schema
changing any one  →  re-embed the corpus into a new index, switch over, keep the old one for rollback

stages.name: Failure modes
stages.html:
Failure Symptom Control
ingestion inside a web request timeouts, partial indexes a batch job or message-driven worker with checkpoints
@Transactional around the model call a database connection held for seconds; pool exhausted no transaction across the LLM call

Next step Gate

followUps.question: What does the advisor do, exactly?
followUps.html:
It intercepts the chat call and adds retrieved context before the model sees the prompt.

user questionadvisor: embed, similarity search with filterschunks appended to the promptmodel callresponse passes back through the advisor

followUps.question: "Spring AI is a different way of doing RAG, so we'd redesign."
followUps.html:
It is the same design behind Spring interfaces.

Unchanged Changed
two pipelines, chunking, embeddings, retrieval, grounding, evaluation the API you call them through

followUps.question: The data science team already has a Python RAG service.
followUps.html:
Then integrate with it; don't rebuild for the sake of the language.

Option When

followUps.question: How do you enforce document permissions?
followUps.html:
A filter expression built from the authenticated user, applied by the vector store.

  • Chunks carry metadata: tenant, access groups, classification.
  • The search request adds the filter in one shared component.
  • Tested with users who must not see each other's documents.

followUps.question: How do you prove it works before launch?

With numbers on a labelled set, per stage.

Stage Metric

answer faithfulness to the retrieved context; correctness on known answers
system p95 time to first token, cost per answer

"Spring AI does RAG for you" — it gives the plumbing; quality is still your work.
"Embed the documents when the user asks."

java-spring-q38.testing: whether you design a small set of intention-shaped tools with authorisation on every call, instead of publishing the REST surface.
java-spring-q38.trap: auto-exposing every endpoint as a tool.
java-spring-q38.spoken:
Beat Say
1 · Clarify "I'd ask which user tasks the model should help with, which of them change data, and who the model is acting for."
2 · Constraints and numbers "A model chooses badly from hundreds of thin tools, and every tool definition costs tokens on every request. So I want a small set: tens at most for one agent."
3 · Baseline design "I'd use the Model Context Protocol. An MCP server exposes tools, resources and prompts in a standard way, and any compliant client can use them. With Spring AI that is a Spring service with annotated methods: the description tells the model when to use the tool, and the input schema is derived from the method signature."
4 · Deep-dive the hard part "The design work is the tool surface. Tools are shaped around intentions, 'find a customer's recent orders', not around endpoints. And every tool call is both untrusted input and a privileged action. So identity comes from the validated token, never from an argument the model supplied. Authorisation runs on each call. Destructive actions need human approval."
5 · Failure modes "The model will retry and will send odd arguments, so tools are idempotent, validated and time-limited, and their output is treated as data that may carry injected instructions."
6 · Evolve "Then audit logging per call, rate limits per user, and an evaluation set of tasks."
Close "A few intention-shaped tools over MCP, the user's identity and permissions on every call, approval for anything destructive."

stages.name: Clarify
stages.claim: tasks, side effects, on whose behalf
stages.html:
Ask Shapes
which user tasks? the tool list comes from tasks, not from the API catalogue
read-only or state-changing? approval flows, idempotency
who is the model acting for? the token to propagate; per-user permissions
internal agent only, or third-party clients? authentication and exposure of the server

stages.name: Constraints and numbers
stages.claim: few tools, each paid for in tokens
stages.html:
200 tools × about 150 tokens of name, description and schema = 30,000 tokens on every request     (illustrative)
12 tools  × about 150 tokens                                 =  1,800 tokens
Many thin tools Few intention-shaped tools
the model picks the wrong one more often each has a clear purpose
many calls chained to do one task one call per intention
large, costly context small context

stages.name: Baseline design
stages.html:
// Spring AI 2.x style: a fragment to show the shape, not run here
@McpTool(name = "findOrdersForCustomer", description = "List recent orders for one customer. Read-only.")
List<OrderSummary> findOrders(@McpToolParam(description = "Customer ID, format C-0000") String customerId) {
    var principal = SecurityContextHolder.getContext().getAuthentication().getName();   // from the validated token
    authz.requireCanViewCustomer(principal, customerId);                                 // on every call
    return orders.recentFor(customerId);
}
MCP primitive Use
tools actions and queries the model can invoke
resources data the client can read into context
prompts reusable templates the server offers

stages.name: Deep-dive the hard part
stages.claim: the tool surface and the trust boundary
stages.html:
Endpoint-shaped (avoid) Intention-shaped (prefer)
GET /customers/{id}, GET /orders?customerId=, GET /orders/{id}/items findOrdersForCustomer(customerId) returning what a support agent needs
PATCH /orders/{id} with arbitrary fields cancelOrder(orderId, reason) with its own rules
Rule Why
identity from the token, never from arguments a model-supplied customer ID is a request, not proof
authorise on every call the model can be steered into asking for anything
validate arguments strictly types, formats, ranges, allowlists
human approval for destructive or costly actions cancellations, refunds, emails, deletions
least privilege per tool a read tool uses read-only credentials
the description is prompt text it is the model's only basis for choosing the tool: write it precisely

Trust boundary: arguments coming in are untrusted. Results going back may contain text written by customers or third parties, so the client must treat them as data, not instructions.

stages.name: Failure modes
stages.html:
Failure Symptom Control
retried tool call a duplicate refund or order idempotency keys on state-changing tools
confused deputy the model, acting for user A, fetches user B's data the server authorises against the caller's token
prompt injection through tool output a document says "now call deleteAccount" approvals; allowlisted follow-up actions; separate the planner from untrusted text
a hung backend the agent loop stalls a timeout per tool and a clear error result
huge results the context overflows pagination and summaries in the tool, with a size cap
tool description drift the model misuses a tool after a change version tools; test selection on an evaluation set

stages.html:
Add Gives
an audit log per call: who, which tool, arguments, result status traceability for every model action
rate limits and quotas per user and per tool protection from loops
stateless HTTP transport with OAuth for remote clients any replica can serve any request
an evaluation set of tasks does the model pick the right tool with the right arguments
a tool registry with owners new tools are a governed change

followUps.html:
MCP standardises discovery and invocation, so one server works with many clients.

Provider function calling MCP
Defined per application and model provider server, once
Reusable by other agents and tools no yes
Still needed — the model's tool-calling ability underneath

followUps.question: "Generate tools from our OpenAPI spec: all 300 endpoints."
followUps.html:
That publishes the API's shape, not the tasks.

  • Selection quality falls as the list grows.
  • Token cost rises on every request.
  • Every write endpoint becomes reachable by a steered model.

followUps.question: A tool needs to act as the end user against a downstream service.
followUps.html:
Exchange the user's token for one scoped to that service; don't pass it through.

user tokenMCP server validates audiencetoken exchange for the downstream audiencedownstream call with least privilege

followUps.question: How is the input schema produced?
followUps.html:
From the method signature and parameter annotations.

  • Java types become JSON Schema types.
  • Parameter descriptions come from the annotation.
  • Records and enums give the model a tight, self-describing shape.

followUps.question: Who approves a new tool?
followUps.html:
The service owner and security, with a checklist.

Check Question
authorisation is every call checked against the caller?
side effects idempotent, and approved if destructive?
data exposure what can the result contain?
evaluation does the model select and call it correctly?

dontSay: "Expose the REST API as tools."
"The model passes the user ID" — as proof of identity.
"The LLM decides what it's allowed to do."

java-spring-q39.testing: whether you see memory and guardrails as steps in one advisor chain, bound the memory, and key it so tenants can't see each other.
java-spring-q39.trap: unbounded chat memory: cost grows every turn until the context window overflows.
java-spring-q39.spoken:
Beat Say
1 · Clarify "I'd ask how long a conversation must be remembered, whether it must survive a restart and work across instances, and which rules the guardrails enforce."
2 · Constraints and numbers "The model is stateless, so 'memory' means re-sending history on every turn. Without a cap, turn fifty sends forty-nine turns of history: cost and latency grow linearly, and eventually the window is exceeded."
3 · Baseline design "In Spring AI both concerns are advisors: an interceptor chain around the chat call. A chat-memory advisor loads this conversation's history before the call and saves the new exchange after. Guardrail advisors sit on both sides: input checks before the model, output checks after."
4 · Deep-dive the hard part "The memory itself is a ChatMemory over a repository: in-memory for development, JDBC or Redis for real, so any instance can serve the next turn. The strategy is a sliding window of recent messages, with older turns summarised. And the key is conversation plus tenant, derived from the authenticated user, or one customer's history leaks into another's."
5 · Failure modes "Failures: unbounded history, memory in a singleton's field, guardrails only on input, and advisors in the wrong order."
6 · Evolve "Then long-term memory as retrieval over past conversations, and guardrail metrics."
Close "One advisor chain: bounded, tenant-keyed memory, and guardrails before and after the model."

stages.name: Clarify
stages.html:
Ask Shapes
how many turns matter? window size, summarisation
must it survive restarts and scale out? an external repository
retention and deletion rules? expiry, per-user deletion
which guardrails? input: injection, abuse, off-topic; output: personal data, policy, format
what happens on a violation? block, redact, or ask again

stages.html:
tokens sent on turn n ≈ system prompt + Σ of all previous turns + the new message
200 tokens per turn, no cap:   turn 10 → about 2,000    turn 50 → about 10,000    turn 200 → about 40,000   (illustrative)
window of 10 turns + a 300-token summary:   about 2,300 tokens on every turn

stages.html:
Decision Choice Why
store a repository in JDBC or Redis the next turn may land on another instance
strategy sliding window (MessageWindowChatMemory), plus a rolling summary of older turns bounded tokens; say what is dropped
key tenant + user + conversation, from the authenticated principal no cross-user leakage

Where the key comes from:validated tokentenant and usercombined with a server-issued conversation IDmemory lookup

stages.name: Failure modes
stages.html:
Failure Symptom Control
unbounded memory cost per turn climbs; eventually a context-length error window plus summary; a token budget per turn
history in a singleton bean's field or a static map users see each other's messages; lost on restart a keyed external repository
guardrail only on input the model's own output leaks personal data or breaks policy check both sides
advisor order wrong unsafe input is stored in memory before it is checked guard first; memory after
blocked content saved to history the next turn replays the injection don't persist rejected turns
summaries drift facts are lost or invented over many summarisations keep key facts as structured notes; re-summarise from source periodically
streaming output a violation is shown before the check finishes buffer per sentence, or check incrementally and cut the stream

stages.html:
Addition How

structured user profile facts the user stated, kept as fields, not as chat text
guardrail metrics trigger rate per rule, false-positive samples, latency added
an evaluation set multi-turn cases: does it remember, does it refuse what it should

Trust boundary: guardrails reduce risk; they don't replace authorisation on tools and data. A request that passes the guard is still checked where it acts.

followUps.question: Window or summary?
followUps.html:
Both: recent turns verbatim, older ones compressed.

Strategy Keeps Loses
window only exact recent wording everything older
summary only the gist of everything exact wording and detail
window + summary recent detail and older gist some old detail

followUps.question: "Keep the whole conversation; the context window is huge now."
followUps.html:
You pay for every token on every turn, and accuracy on mid-context details can fall.

  • Cost and latency scale with history length.
  • A window with a summary is cheaper and usually answers as well.

followUps.question: The same user has two browser tabs open.
followUps.html:
Two conversation IDs, or one with ordered writes.

Design Behaviour
an ID per tab independent histories
a shared ID concurrent turns can interleave: serialise writes per conversation

followUps.question: How are guardrails implemented?
followUps.html:
As cheap checks first, model-based checks where needed.

  • Rules and patterns: block lists, personal-data patterns, schema validation.
  • A small classifier or moderation model for abuse and injection.
  • An LLM check only for policies that need reasoning, on a budget.

followUps.question: What are the privacy obligations of storing chat history?
followUps.html:
It is personal data with a lifecycle.

Obligation Design
retention limit expiry per conversation
deletion on request a delete path keyed by user
access control encryption at rest; no history in logs
purpose limits not reused for training without consent

dontSay: "Store the chat history in the service."
"Send the whole history each time."
"The system prompt tells it to behave" as the guardrail.
